notes: Source claim: sendmail is presented as the first and still most prevalent Internet mail transfer agent, begun in 1980 as delivermail to forward messages among incompatible networks; the chapter cites over 800 million Internet hosts as of January 2011 (lines 11-14, 41-47).

Source claim: the setting was UUCP, the Arpanet, BerkNET and XNS, with OSI/X.400 as a rival; machines had 16-bit address spaces, no threads, no kernel file locking, no sockets and no public-key encryption, and message formats were barely standardized (lines 20-38, 50-53).

Source claim: the design principles reduce to doing as little as possible — accept one finite part-time programmer, do not redesign MUAs or the local mail store, adapt to existing transports, change little, think about reliability early, and leave functionality out until needed (lines 56-104).

Source claim: development proceeded in waves: delivermail with compiled-in routing; sendmail 3-5 with runtime configuration, address rewriting and embedded SMTP (VRFY/EXPN, immediate RCPT rejection); vendor forks and IDA/KJS in the chaos years; sendmail 8 with a unified map mechanism and m4 configuration; commercial-era TLS, SMTP AUTH and milters; versions 6 and 7 were skipped (lines 107-194).

Source claim: configuration syntax was constrained by a small 16-bit parser, and the tab as an active separator was copied from make and later regretted; rewriting rules were chosen over regular expressions because email addresses contain regex metacharacters and need word boundaries and quoting, and arbitrary backtracking also helped parse header addresses (lines 203-247).

Source claim: SMTP and queueing were embedded rather than split into a separate mailer to permit piggybacked RCPTs, per-recipient status, VRFY/EXPN alias access and graceful handling of transient failures; the queue used two flat files per job and hit a performance knee around 10,000 messages (lines 250-277).

Source claim: Postel's law was applied deliberately — add a missing From:, convert line endings, repair malformed addresses — which the author judges right for the time but problematic once standards matured; the m4 configuration began as an 80/20 convenience and became a de facto assembly language with the .mc file as source (lines 280-313).

Source claim: Internet-scale design must balance client and server interests rather than favor one side; milter runs filters out of process and synchronously with SMTP, and was kept out of sendmail's address space for security, fault isolation and debuggability (lines 322-348).

Source claim: security history includes root privileges, the 'distrust all input' rule, ownership/mode checks and DontBlameSendmail, abuse of VRFY/EXPN, and joe-jobs versus bounce reliability; later evolution made filtering the first priority, added early envelope rulesets, TCP/IP-specific peeking, TLS, pipelining and the submission port (lines 361-442).

Source claim: in hindsight the author would fix the configuration syntax and tab earlier, reject bad input sooner, avoid null-terminated strings, separate mailbox names from Unix user ids, and keep rewriting rules, syslog and C, while avoiding XML as a configuration language (lines 445-526).

Representation observation: footnote markers are flattened into words and numbers, both example tables and the single code block lost their layout, and the file contains only the eight opening chrome lines; no prose section is missing and the heading set matches the live HTML.

notes: Source claim: SnowFlock adds VM Cloning as a cloud API call so applications can invoke cloud resources like a syscall, with allocation, cluster membership and application logic combined in one logical operation; clones inherit parent state including OS and application caches and join a private network (lines 11-32).

Source claim: the central tradeoff is eager versus lazy state replication. Eager migration-style copying gives the best initial performance but delays instantiation; SnowFlock's lazy approach copies only what is needed to start, minimizing latency and copying only used state, at the cost of on-demand stalls (lines 35-50).

Source claim: VM Fork differs from Unix fork in three ways — it duplicates the whole VM including memory, processes, devices and local disk; it spawns many copies in parallel; and it can target distinct physical hosts (lines 53-56).

Source claim: the design rests on virtualization, lazy propagation, multicast, page faults and copy-on-write, and comprises six components: VM descriptor, mcdist, memory server, memtap, optional clone enlightenment and the per-host control stack (lines 59-88).

Source claim: the architectural descriptor is fast to create (about 200 ms), small (about 1 MB for a 1 GB VM) and turns into a running clone in under a second (typically about 800 ms); SnowFlock requires privileged host access, so it cannot be used as a tenant in a public cloud such as EC2 (lines 96-117).

Source claim: the memserver freezes the parent's memory using Xen-assisted copy-on-write; mcdist uses IP multicast with lockstep detection, receive-rate flow control and an end-game unicast fallback; the virtual disk is frozen, copy-on-write, multicast at 4 KB granularity and stored as a transient sparse file (lines 120-168).

Source claim: each clone's memtap handles first-access faults using a page-presence bitmap and atomic x86 bit operations, avoiding locks across hypervisor, memtap and guest; clone enlightenment lets the guest mark pages that will be overwritten (allocator pages) as present so they are never fetched (lines 171-198).

Source claim: the API is sf_request_ticket, sf_clone, sf_checkpoint_parent, sf_create_clones, sf_exit, sf_join and sf_kill, marshalled through XenStore to per-host SFLD daemons, with a central SFMD deferring allocation to existing cluster managers such as Sun Grid Engine or Platform EGO (lines 201-227).

Source claim: cloning requires identity mutations — a private virtual network, per-clone IDs mapped to IP and MAC addresses, synthetic DHCP responses and layer-2 isolation via dedicated MAC OUIs; a router VM provides NAT, firewalling and throttling and is acknowledged as a scalability bottleneck (lines 228-246).

Source claim: the conclusion claims dozens of clones in seconds, 20x faster instantiation and warm-cache benefits; the reported lessons are KISS (on-demand paging and the page bitmap) and that scale exposes new bottlenecks, with mcdist outperforming TCP-based distribution at hundreds of clones (lines 249-261).

sections.title: 20.3.3. Requesting Channels, Channel Properties and Dispatching
20.7. A Brief Look Inside a Connection Manager

notes: Source claim: Telepathy is a modular real-time communications framework covering voice, video, text and file transfer; its distinguishing idea is communications as a service shared by many applications through D-Bus, including Tubes, and it was created by Robert McQueen in 2005 (lines 11-17).

Source claim: D-Bus is an asynchronous shared message bus with system, per-user session, private and peer-to-peer variants; libraries such as libdbus, GDBus, QtDBus and python-dbus marshal types and publish objects, while the daemon handles message passing and name registration (lines 20-32).

Source claim: the framework splits into Connection Managers, an Account Manager, a Channel Dispatcher and clients; Mission Control is one process providing the Account Manager and Channel Dispatcher; the split buys robustness, replaceability, language, license and interface independence, and privilege separation (lines 35-68).

Source claim: D-Bus objects are strict namespaced paths implementing interfaces; Telepathy simulates object types through paths, base interfaces and a ChannelType property, and publishes optional interfaces through an Interfaces property because common introspection assumes a class has a fixed interface set (lines 76-112); the D-Bus IDL was also extended with documentation, rationale, introduction and deprecation versions, exceptions and named simple types, structs, maps, enums and flags, partly to strengthen generated language bindings (lines 76-130).

Source claim: handles are unsigned integers assigned per connection so the tuple (connection, handle type, handle) identifies a contact or room; protocol-specific normalization makes string comparison wrong, so only handles should be compared (lines 136-143).

Source claim: service discovery is stateless: clients and Connection Managers announce well-known name prefixes on the bus, and an interested component asks the daemon what is running; connections are themselves advertised services, which lets the Account Manager re-associate after a crash (lines 148-164).

Source claim: traffic reduction replaced many getter calls with D-Bus properties and GetAll, added immutable channel properties to the NewChannels signal, queued avatar fetches behind one AvatarRetrieved signal, and introduced the Contacts interface and GetContactAttributes to batch roster data (lines 169-231).

Source claim: channels are requested as maps of interface-qualified properties, with create versus ensure semantics; new channels announce immutable properties, and the Channel Dispatcher routes to Observers, then Approvers, then a Handler, using client filters matched against immutable properties (lines 242-368).

Source claim: language bindings are optional and split into generated low-level and hand-written high-level layers; all bus calls are asynchronous because D-Bus is, and the pseudo-synchronous style was removed from telepathy-glib after causing unresponsiveness, message reordering and deadlock (lines 374-424).

Source claim: high-level proxies have explicit readiness features (core state plus optional contact info, capabilities, location, chat states, avatars); robustness relies on state recovery at Mission Control start, client respawn and channel reissue, message acknowledgement, and Connection respawn (lines 427-466).

Source claim: sidecars are plugin-provided D-Bus objects beside a Connection for protocol extensions, a generalization of OLPC XEP support in Telepathy-Gabble; Connection Managers use base classes and mixins, including TpPresenceMixin to keep the old complex presence interface working over SimplePresence (lines 471-503). The closing lessons are to use properties/GetAll, announce immutable properties, batch with Contacts, avoid ill-fitting abstractions such as contact-list channels, and design the API for future needs (lines 508-522).

Source claim: the protocol is a hierarchy of frames with a base type plus added data; Header splits into Request and Response, with OK, Fail and Sequence responses; numerical IDs are addressed by Get With ID, slot variants and ID-sequence exchanges; transport may be TCP, HTTP-tunnelled or SSL (lines 138-156).

Source claim: object, order and resource frames follow the same request/response pattern; the order model evolved from one queue per object with Outcome/Result frames, to Outcome folded into Order, to a refactored Order Queue with Insert Order and Probe Order (lines 206-218).

Source claim: design manipulation covers categories, components, properties and designs; Property rank prevents circular dependencies (a function may not depend on a property of lower or equal rank); components carry TPCL Requirements and properties carry Calculate and Requirements functions; Design frames add owner, instance count, component counts and feedback (lines 224-302).

Source claim: the administration protocol runs on a separate port with Connect/Login, pushed Log Message frames and command descriptions fetched by Get Command Description IDs; tpserver-cpp persistence is an abstract class with modular MySQL and SQLite back ends updated continuously as state changes (lines 305-335).

Source claim: TPCL is a Scheme R5RS subset chosen for simplicity, embedding precedent, interpreter availability and documentation, and lets clients validate designs locally; BattleXML splits media and battle definitions for two viewers; metaserver-lite is PHP, updated by HTTP, expires listings after ten minutes, and can return Game frames to clients (lines 338-396).

Source claim: single-player mode uses XML DTD component metadata aggregated into server, ruleset and AI-client dictionaries, then launches a local server and AI clients and connects normally; saved games copy a live SQLite database and add a configuration table; the authors' lessons favour small iterations and protocol versioning, and name the binary protocol and excessive flexibility as mistakes (lines 398-475).

Source claim: visualization covers the whole transformation of data into sensory output, including meshes, scalars, vectors, tensors, normals and texture coordinates; VTK also addresses abstract information visualization, and is architected as interchangeable components feeding dataflow pipelines (lines 26-32).

notes: Source claim: the Battle for Wesnoth is a turn-based fantasy strategy game released under a GPL2 license, with more than four million downloads at the time of writing; the chapter's stated aim is to show how its development model let volunteers of widely different skill levels contribute (lines 17-24).
Source claim: the engine is about 200,000 lines of C++ and ships with roughly 250,000 lines of WML content; functionality once hard-coded in C++ has increasingly moved into WML (line 32).

Source claim: the project minimises dependencies for portability but relies on SDL for video, I/O and event handling, plus SDL_Mixer, SDL_Image and SDL_Net, and on Boost, Pango/Cairo, zlib, Python/Lua and GNU gettext (lines 38-58).

Source claim: subsystems are deliberately segmented - WML parser/preprocessor, I/O, GUI, display, AI, hexagonal pathfinding, map generation and game-flow modules - so a contributor can change one area without damaging the rest; display and 'play game' are the largest and have risked the Blob anti-pattern (lines 63-91).

Source claim: XML was considered but rejected for WML because a more relaxed, non-technical syntax was wanted; WML has elements and string-to-string attributes but no text nodes, and all game data is presented to the engine as one conceptual document (lines 100-141).

Source claim: a preprocessor supplies file/directory includes, macros and conditional symbols used for difficulty; changing a preprocessor symbol forces the entire WML document to be reloaded and reprocessed (lines 144-197).

Source claim: the single multi-megabyte WML document can take up to a minute to load and consumes substantial memory; mitigations are campaign-specific #ifdef content and a cache of the fully preprocessed document keyed by the active symbol set and invalidated by file timestamps (lines 200-203).

Source claim: Wesnoth deliberately avoids unit inheritance; a unit instance refers to an immutable unit_type, abilities are flags interpreted by engine code (for example pathfinding checks 'skirmisher'), and attacks are attack_type lists (lines 212-224).

Source claim: traits and equipment are WML-defined modifications to unit statistics, including selected attack types; fully WML-defined abilities were rejected because WML would become a programming language and because the C++ AI would still need to understand each ability (lines 227-233).

Source claim: multiplayer actions are serialised as WML nodes, and a complete replay is the initial state plus the command log; a thin wesnothd relay distributes commands over TCP, observers receive initial state plus history, and server version segmentation makes divergent rules visible; the project consciously does not attempt strong cheat prevention (lines 239-264).

Source claim: the authors present accessibility as a series of compromises that look inelegant in code - WML's inefficient syntax is criticised internally - but credit it with hundreds of user-made campaigns and with drawing people into programming; they caution that Wesnoth's open-source and GPL setting limits how far the lessons generalise (lines 270-279).

sections.title: 9.1.1. What Does Continuous Integration Software Do?

notes: Source claim: CI systems build and test software automatically and regularly; benefits include cross-platform testing, slow or data-intensive tests, legacy-platform checks, detection of infrequently failing tests and release production, and CI is often a step toward continuous deployment (line 11).

Source claim: the chapter contrasts four systems - Buildbot (master/slave), CDash (reporting server), Jenkins (hybrid) and Pony-Build (decentralised Python reporting server) - as extremes and a foil (lines 17-35).
Source claim: CI architectures are dominated by two extremes, central master/slave control and client-contributed reporting; known systems combine features from both (line 23).

Source claim: Buildbot's buildmaster schedules builds and buildslaves execute them over persistent connections; locks make system-integration coordination easy, but new slaves cannot attach dynamically, clients are fully controlled by the master, build products cannot easily be returned, and slave load is not reported (lines 26, 114-132).

Source claim: CDash is a reporting server for CMake/CTest clients; clients decide when to build and upload XML reports, which permits volunteer and cloud builds but gives up central scheduling, progress reports and a guaranteed response to a check-in (lines 29, 141-150).

Source claim: CDash added an '@Home' mode in which clients poll for build requests and return results; at the time of writing (October 2010) requests were manual and clients had to be connected (line 153).

Source claim: Jenkins (Hudson until early 2011) is a Java hybrid that can build locally, coordinate remote builds over master-initiated SSH or client-initiated JNLP, and passively receive results; its plugin architecture supports third-party result and binary return, while its locks plugin was immature in January 2011 (lines 159-171).

Source claim: Pony-Build separates a results server, independent clients holding build configuration, and an optional reporting server, linked by webhooks, XML-RPC and PubSubHubbub; this buys language independence, testability, easy modification and low server load, but makes build requests, distributed locking and real-time monitoring hard (lines 180-211).

Source claim: the feature inventory includes checkout/update, abstract recipes, stored checkout/build/test status, release packages, multi-architecture builds, resource management, external-resource coordination and progress reports; external interactions cover notification, build information, build requests and remote control (lines 66-99).

Source claim: recipes are hard because they must be platform-independent yet customisable, and trust is a second problem because recipes execute arbitrary code; the authors suggest community-standard recipes or digitally signed recipes (lines 220-235).

Source claim: the authors judge a loosely coupled RPC/webhook model easy and flexible except for build coordination, so model choice should follow project needs; they call 'architecture dictates function' nonsense and argue architecture canalises development while contributor self-selection reinforces the fit (lines 241-250, 268-280).

Source claim: future wishes are a language-agnostic recipe DSL, common build/test reporting formats such as TAP or JUnit XML, and richer platform introspection hooks (lines 258-262). notes: Source claim: six principles—availability, performance, reliability, scalability, manageability and cost—guide web distributed design, and they conflict; adding servers can reduce manageability and raise cost (lines 25-41).

Source claim: image hosting separates upload/write from read; long-lived uploads consume web-server connections (about 500 by default) while reads can be asynchronous, cached or compressed, so splitting services lets each scale independently (lines 56-105).

Source claim: Flickr instead shards by user, which limits outage blast radius and follows user growth but complicates cross-dataset queries; the chapter says neither design is universally right (lines 108-111).
Source claim: redundancy of data and services removes single points of failure; shared-nothing nodes avoid a central coordinator, and replicas should be geographically separated (lines 117-129).
Source claim: horizontal partitioning needs a stable name or ID-to-server mapping (consistent hashing or ranges), and introduces data-locality and race/inconsistency risks (lines 135-156).

Source claim: caches exploit locality; local caches suffer misses under random load balancing; global caches centralize storage and retrieval while distributed caches shard by consistent hashing; Memcached and Facebook's multi-layer caching are examples (lines 189-231).

Source claim: proxies filter, log or transform and can collapse identical or spatially adjacent requests; a cache should sit in front of the proxy to avoid added latency; Squid and Varnish are named (lines 240-258).
Source claim: indexes trade write and storage overhead for read speed; an inverted index maps words to books, and a 100-million-book estimate yields over 1 TB for one entry per word (lines 264-294).

Source claim: load balancers distribute connections by random, round-robin or utilization; sticky sessions conflict with failover, and automatic removal of slow nodes can amplify overload without monitoring (lines 303-321).

sections.title: Task Priorities and the Ready List

notes: Source claim: embedded systems are special-purpose computers (TV remote, GPS, watch, pacemaker), typically smaller, slower and cheaper; real-time systems must guarantee that work happens within a time bound, with a pacemaker as the motivating example; typical low-end hardware is an 8-bit 25 MHz CPU with a few KB of RAM and 32 KB of flash (lines 32-38).

Source claim: the minimum core is three .c files plus headers, just under 9,000 lines including comments and blanks, producing a binary under 10 KB; roughly half the core handles tasks, about 40% communication, and about 6% is the hardware shim (lines 44-53).

Source claim: the hardware-independent core calls macros such as portENTER_CRITICAL that portmacro.h defines per compiler and architecture, with port.c/portasm.s holding the implementation; basic types and the tick type are likewise defined per port, so retargeting means replacing only the portable layer (lines 59-113).

Source claim: priorities range from 0 to configMAX_PRIORITIES-1 and the ready list is an array of lists indexed by priority; the system tick calls vTaskSwitchContext, whose loop walks down from uxTopReadyPriority to the highest non-empty list and listGET_OWNER_OF_NEXT_ENTRY advances pxIndex for round-robin among equal-priority tasks (lines 122-166).

Source claim: the TCB holds stack top/start, stack-growth-dependent overflow fields, two list items, priority and base priority; a task has four states (running, ready, suspended, blocked) but no state field - state is implied by which list contains the task (lines 178-240).

Source claim: xTaskCreate allocates a TCB and stack, then initialises the stack to resemble a context-switch frame (pxPortInitialiseStack on ARM Cortex-M3 stores xPSR, PC, LR, R0 and reserves R1-R12); interrupts are disabled while the ready lists are updated, and first-task creation initialises all scheduler lists (lines 246-288).

Source claim: lists are circular doubly linked, sorted high-to-low by xItemValue, with pvOwner pointing back to the owning TCB, pvContainer identifying the containing list, and xListEnd as a maximum-value sentinel; pxIndex makes the list itself remember the traversal position (lines 294-367).

Source claim: queues keep head/tail/write/read pointers and two waiting lists; insertion deep-copies items so the queue outlives caller variables; blocking operations take a timeout and a task may still fail after unblocking if another task or interrupt changes the queue before it runs (lines 382-448).

Source claim: a semaphore is an N-item queue with zero item size whose uxMessagesWaiting count is the only state; a mutex overloads pcHead/pcTail as uxQueueType/pxMutexHolder via #defines, marks itself with uxQueueType=0, records the holder, and implements priority inheritance by raising a lower-priority holder to the waiter's priority (lines 454-499).

Source claim: the conclusion explicitly excludes memory allocation, ISRs, debugging and MPU support, and refers readers to Richard Barry's book for setup and usage (line 508). sections.title: Target Vectors and the Target Stack
Make a Plan, but Expect It to Change
Things Would Be Great If We Were Infinitely Intelligent
Learn to Live with Incomplete Transitions

notes: Source claim: GDB is a symbolic debugger for compiled imperative languages (C, C++, Ada, Fortran), built as an interactive toolbox for an unpredictable request sequence; it must still work with optimized binaries and with symbols that are missing, stale or incorrect (lines 20-46).

Source claim: GDB dates from about 1985, written by Richard Stallman alongside GCC; the earliest readily available releases are from 1988, nearly all code has since been rewritten, and the original goals were modest with later growth into unplanned environments (lines 55-58).

Source claim: the architecture has a symbol side (names, types, lines, registers, expression parsing, source listing) and a target side (start/stop, memory and register access, signals), tied together by a command interpreter and execution control loop; native debugging mostly wraps ptrace, cross-debugging sends packets over a wire (lines 64-74).

Source claim: printing a variable parses an expression tree, resolves the symbol to an address, reads target memory and formats the bytes; source/assembly display joins source reads with line-number tables; single-stepping executes one instruction, compares the PC with the current line's address range and repeats until the line changes, which handles jumps and calls without decoding the instruction set but is slow on some embedded targets (lines 80-102).

Source claim: portability separates host, target and native definitions, with target definitions split into architecture and native subclasses; autoconf probes host properties, architecture definitions moved from macros to gdbarch objects for variants and multi-architecture support, affecting perhaps 80,000 lines and reaching up to 130 methods/variables for a complex target (lines 108-121, 242-248).

Source claim: key data structures include breakpoints shared by watchpoints/catchpoints/tracepoints, symbol tables that can reach multiple gigabytes, bidirectional line tables, explicit frame objects introduced in 2002, expression trees that union all supported languages, and value structs recording r-value/l-value and lazy construction (lines 128-177).

Source claim: the symbol side uses BFD to read a.out, COFF and ELF; minimal symbols carry names and addresses, detailed formats such as DWARF or stabs add types; partial symbol tables scan only globally visible symbols at startup and fill in function-local detail on demand, reducing startup from minutes to seconds for large programs (lines 182-206).

Source claim: the target side was redesigned in 1990 around target vectors (about 40, several dozen function pointers each) and a target stack with strata so process-like vectors can override file-like ones; the remote protocol uses simple checksummed packets such as $g#67, has few required and many optional packets, and is implemented by debugging stubs or by GDBserver, a native proxy about ten times smaller than GDB (lines 227-326).

Source claim: interfaces include a readline-based CLI with cascaded command tables, the Machine Interface (MI) with quoted fields and sequence identifiers for programmatic clients such as Eclipse, plus the TUI and GDBtk; no graphical interface has become universally accepted (lines 335-394).

Source claim: GDB moved in 1999 from a cathedral model with a handful of Cygnus committers to a public repository with dozens of maintainers and 100+ commits per week; the DejaGNU/expect suite had about 18,000 test cases at the end of 2011, with 10-20 failures typical for a native trunk snapshot (lines 403-421).

Source claim (lessons): open development increased patch volume without hurting quality; plans are useful but dates should not be forced and obsolete plans (libgdb) should be dropped; incomplete transitions are normal; developers should not mold their thinking to existing code (lines 430-484).

sections.title: GHC as a Library: The GHC API

notes: Source claim: GHC began in the early 1990s as a UK-government-funded academic project with three goals - a free, robust, portable, high-performance Haskell compiler; a modular foundation others can extend; and learning how real programs behave - and has run for over 20 years with roughly two or three active developers and hundreds of contributors (lines 11-26).

Source claim: Haskell is purely functional, lazy and strongly typed with type inference; monads were the solution that integrated input/output without sacrificing purity, and laziness also blocks impure features (lines 32-42).

Source claim: GHC divides into the compiler, the boot libraries it depends on (so it can bootstrap) and the C runtime system; these map to compiler/, libraries/ and rts/, and the RTS handles GC, scheduling, profiling and exceptions and is linked into every compiled program (lines 51-60).

Source claim: measured compiler size grew from 28,275 to 139,955 lines between 1992 and 2011 (4.9x) while the RTS grew only from 43,865 to 48,450 (1.10x); the type checker added over 20,000 lines, new code generators and GHCi added about 28,000, and the build system is about 6,000 lines of make on its fourth rewrite (lines 69-85).

Source claim: the compiler comprises a compilation manager, Hsc for one Haskell file, and a pipeline of external tools; it is also a library with an API. Phases run parser (HsSyn RdrName via Alex/Happy), renamer (Name), type checker (Id), desugarer to Core, about six other Core optimisation passes with the Simplifier between them, then STG, Cmm and one of native, LLVM or C code generation (lines 91-188).

Source claim: Core (System FC) is a tiny explicitly typed lambda calculus with casts/coercions; GHC type-checks the full source before desugaring rather than after, and runs the Core type checker Lint after passes (-dcore-lint), which catches type errors close to the offending optimisation and independently audits type inference; Core has changed by exactly one major feature in 20 years (lines 197-258).

Source claim: GHC avoids symbol tables: an Id carries its Type, which reaches TyCons and DataCons cyclically, so most queries are field accesses; the cost is that changing a variable's information requires traversing and replacing its occurrences, which the simplifier does routinely (lines 261-296).

Source claim: GHC inlines aggressively across modules using .hi interface files that include small function bodies and INLINE pragmas; this yields fast libraries but makes the ABI depend on inlined code, so library upgrades normally require recompiling clients (lines 302-342).

Source claim: extensibility comes from user rewrite rules (fold/build fuses map/map; about 100 rules in base, dozens in vector), Core-to-Core compiler plugins loaded from object files with annotations, the GHC API used by Haddock, Leksah and hint, and the package system (Cabal library, package database, Hackage, cabal tool) hosting over 3,000 packages (lines 357-456).

Source claim: the RTS is built on a block layer with blocks sized in multiples of 4 KB and bdescr metadata, allocGroup/freeGroup in O(1), 1 MB-aligned allocation and linked block chains, which gives portability and enabled a simple parallel GC; lightweight green threads are multiplexed M:N onto OS threads, use Capabilities, support foreign calls and bound threads, and switch only at allocation safe points, so allocation-free loops can starve the scheduler (lines 485-558).

Source claim (practice): GHC uses headed Notes (about 800) rather than interleaved comments; refactoring is sustained by modularity, strong types and purity; mutation in FastString/NameCache blocked parallel compilation and top-level flag constants broke multi-module compilation; the RTS is kept small, guarded by assertions, and checked with an expensive sanity mode that scans the heap for dangling pointers before and after GC (lines 570-700).

Representation observation: Figure 5.2 is caption-only while the live page has one image; Figures 5.1 and 5.3 are flattened tables at lines 70-71 and 197. Inference (reader): the chapter is a design retrospective by the two main authors, not an independent performance evaluation.

sections.title: 6.5. The Repository, Index and Working Areas

notes: Source claim: Git began in 2005 after BitMover announced it would revoke licences for some Linux kernel developers; Torvalds' stated goal was to be the anti-CVS, with three usability goals - distributed workflows like BitKeeper, safeguards against content corruption and high performance (lines 29-44).

Source claim: a VCS has three core requirements - store content, track changes/history, distribute content and history - and the third is not universal; Git uses a DAG for both content snapshots and commit history, while delta-based changesets are the common alternative (lines 73-111).

Source claim: distribution is local-only, central-server or distributed; the Subversion-versus-Git walkthrough (Alex, a 1 MB file) contrasts a central delta commit with a local full-blob commit plus an explicit push, noting Git's extra moving parts buy workflow flexibility (lines 117-141).

Source claim: the toolkit splits into plumbing (DAG manipulation) and porcelain (user commands); because the Git binary calls die() it is not reentrant, so GUIs and long-running services must fork/exec, which motivated linkable-library work (lines 150-159).

Source claim: .git holds configuration, lifecycle hooks, the future index, the object database and refs; the index is the staging area between working directory and repository, and checkout/add/commit interactions are enumerated and demonstrated (lines 216-247, 256-288).

Source claim: Git has four primitive object types - tree, blob, commit, tag - each with type, size and content, addressed by a 40-digit SHA whose identity and corruption-detection properties carry the distributed and integrity goals (lines 297-317).

Source claim: pack files use an index of offsets; version 2 moved per-object CRC checksums into the index, lifted the 4 GB limit and appends a 20-byte SHA-1 of the ordered object IDs to detect pack corruption (lines 326-335).

Source claim: linear-history VCSs such as Subversion cannot record that changesets from another branch are now contained in trunk; Git merge commits name their parents, but determining exactly which commits each branch contains remains hard, with cherry-pick as the simple-case tool (lines 341-359).

Source claim: follow-on work includes libgit2 and JGit, plus experimental object-database backends (Cassandra, HBase, Memcached/Redis/SQLite/MySQL); the author argues 'Git' is now the repository format and protocol more than the CLI (lines 365-389).

Source claim: lessons learned are the missing linkable library hurting IDE integration, early shell-script commands hurting Windows portability, and plumbing complexity confusing new users (lines 395-404).

Inference: the chapter is a designer's tour, not a measurement study; efficiency claims such as delta storage being 'much more efficient' or DAG ancestry being efficient are qualitative, and no benchmark, timing or corpus is reported.

notes: Source claim: GPSD is a mid-sized suite of about 43 KLOC, mainly C and Python, with a stable core of about three developers; it supports roughly 20 sensor protocols and reports them as JSON on TCP port 2947, with shared-memory and D-Bus alternatives (lines 11-17, 35, 50).

Source claim: the stated design theme is hiding device-dependent protocol ugliness behind a simple client interface talking to a zero-configuration service; client libraries let the client API stay stable while the reporting protocol grows (lines 35, 44, 53).

Source claim: the internals divide into four layers - per-chipset drivers exposed as a C struct of data and method pointers modelled on Unix device drivers, a packet sniffer state machine, a core library managing a device session, and a multiplexer (gpsd.c) handling clients and hotplug (lines 68-98).

Source claim: the first three layers link into libgpsd and are used directly by tools such as gpsmon and gpsctl; system integrators can drop unused drivers from embedded builds, and contributed drivers show the driver API is usable outside the core team (lines 92, 101-104).

Source claim: the daemon selects over clients, sensors, a control socket and DGPS/NTRIP servers treated as sensors; a watch request opens devices, otherwise they stay closed but listed; reports leave through socket, shared-memory or D-Bus exporters (lines 116-145).

Source claim: partition discipline is enforced by rejecting patches that leak input-source details upward where avoidable; the accepted exceptions are probe strings and the -b no-baud-change option, needed because some cheap devices misbehave, while a device with invalid NMEA checksums was refused rather than weakening validation or adding a forced-type switch (lines 160-178).

Source claim: zero configuration means no dotfile, sniffed protocols, autobaud and hotplug scripts; the author argues configuration that can be edited must be edited, adding setup burden (lines 184-196).

Source claim: embedded goals produced a 69K minimum static build versus about 418K with all drivers (June 2011, 64-bit x86), CPU use near profiler noise on FPU-less ARM, and a split between a C daemon and Python test/utility code; the author states measurements should replace guesses (lines 208-223).

Source claim: the original one-letter-key request/response protocol ran out of command space and mismatched streaming sensors; JSON with a class attribute restored extensibility, at the cost of a larger parser, so GPSD wrote a static-storage subset parser in about 600 lines and kept a shared-memory path for tight deployments (lines 229-247, 292-296).

Source claim: the daemon never uses malloc/calloc, which removes leak and double-free classes and improves static analysis; the project runs splint, cppcheck and Coverity plus regression tests over more than 70 sensor logs, and the author reports an empty bug tracker and no crash bug in six years as of July 2011 (lines 265-280).

Source claim: lessons are to design for extensibility and to ship client-side libraries; the author defends scope growth by cost - a new driver is usually under 1 KLOC, Marine AIS about 3 KLOC, drivers plus sniffer and report generators about 18 KLOC of 43 KLOC, so the framework and tests dominate (lines 307-318).

Inference: the defect-rate and footprint claims are author-reported project measurements without an independent audit or a date-stamped method, and the chapter's date (mid-2011) means its 'empty tracker' and build sizes are historical snapshots. Representation note: both figures are caption-only, there are no code blocks, lines 1-9 are chrome, and the live HTML checked 2026-10-24 contains the same 10 sections and 2 figures.

notes: Source claim: the Iron languages are dynamic languages targeting the CLR and built on the DLR; IronPython and IronRuby are used in dozens of projects, and the DLR ships as part of .NET Framework and Mono (line 11).

Source claim: Jim Hugunin, already author of Jython, prototyped Python on the CLR expecting to write a critique, found it about 1.7x faster than C Python on pystone, was hired by Microsoft, and the DLR was factored out of IronPython; Microsoft announced DLR/IronPython 2.0/IronRuby in April 2007 and stopped developing the Iron languages in October 2010 (lines 20-30).

Source claim: the CLR assumes types never change at runtime, so the DLR supplies a shared dynamic object model with language-specific binders, call-site caching and expression trees; it is implemented purely as libraries, needs no CLR change and runs on .NET 2.0 (lines 39-51).

Source claim: every implementation has a language-specific front end and the DLR provides a common backend from expression trees to IL, then JIT to machine code; runtime-evaluated code follows the same path at the eval call site (line 57).

Source claim: IronPython uses a hand-written tokenizer and an LL(1) recursive-descent parser; IronRuby generates a table-based LALR(1) parser with GPPG from Parser.y (540 states, over 45,000 transitions). The stated trade-off is hand-modifiable clarity versus grammar readability plus a third-party tool dependency (lines 66-75).

Source claim: DLR expression trees are low-level and language-independent, custom nodes reduce recursively to intrinsic nodes, and the immutable tree is rewritten through the Visitor-pattern ExpressionVisitor, which must rebuild parents when it changes a child (lines 87-93).

Source claim: expression trees run in a stack-based interpreter first (LightLambdaExpression), and after a default threshold of 32 executions are reduced, compiled to a DynamicMethod on a background thread and swapped into the call site; compilation or interpretation can be disabled by option (lines 102-114).

Source claim: every dynamic operation becomes a call site with a language binder; rules live in L0 (Target), L1 (10 rules) and L2 (128 rules shared on the binder), motivated by roughly 10 ns for a type check versus 80 microseconds to compile a rule, about 1 KB per variation, and profiling that showed few sites exceed 10 variations (lines 146-158).

Source claim: the meta-object protocol treats all object models as Smalltalk-style message passing over Get/Set/Delete member and index, Invoke, CreateInstance, Convert and unary/binary operations; DynamicMetaObject plus IDynamicMetaObjectProvider carry language semantics, and host binders fall back to target-language then host-language binding (lines 184-220).

Source claim: hosting exposes ScriptRuntime, per-language ScriptEngine, ScriptSource/SourceUnit and ScriptScope; engines are thread-safe when each thread has its own scope, and scopes both hold variables and isolate scripts, with LanguageContext supplying all language behaviour (lines 235-250).

Source claim: DLR parts split between the CLR (call sites, expression trees, binders, code generation, meta objects) and the IronLanguages project (hosting, interpreter), packaged as Microsoft.Scripting and Microsoft.Dynamic; lessons cite agile development with CI from day one, a 12-second DLR suite versus a 45-minute IronPython suite, and hosting APIs that never entered the .NET Framework so PowerShell 3 uses different ones (lines 259-277).

Inference: the 1.7x pystone result, nanosecond/microsecond costs and suite durations are author-reported figures from project history rather than reproducible measurements in the chapter; the claim that 'a state machine is always the right answer' (line 78) is rhetorical, not evidenced. sections.title: The Inner Workings of the Pipeline

notes: Source claim: ITK is an image-analysis library initiated and mainly funded by the US National Library of Medicine, built by a consortium of universities, companies and individual contributors; development is dated to 1999 in the introduction and to 2000 in the refactoring section, and a post-10th-anniversary refactor is described (lines 14, 539).
Source claim: the stated architectural features are modularity, data pipeline, factories, IO factories, streaming, reusability and maintainability (lines 49-64).

Source claim: modularity operates at filter, filter-family (module) and group levels; about 700 filters, about 120 modules at first mention and 124 modules in 13 groups later, with modules mapping to source directories and compiled libraries and containing filter code, build/dependency configuration and unit tests (lines 75-93).

Source claim: third-party image-format libraries (HDF5, PNG, TIFF, JPEG, OpenJPEG) account for about 56% of ITK's size and were partitioned during modularization; module size distribution was used to monitor the refactor (lines 96-99).

Source claim: the pipeline is built from DataObject (data) and ProcessObject (algorithm) abstractions; SetInput()/GetOutput() calls connect a downstream ProcessObject to the upstream DataObject, output ownership stays with the producer, inputs are const, and the pipeline is a pull pipeline (lines 153-186, 230).

Source claim: one Update() at the terminal filter triggers four passes - UpdateOutputInformation, PropagateRequestedRegion, UpdateOutputData and GenerateData - the first three upstream and the last downstream by call timing; the writer requests 500x500 and the median filter asks upstream for 502x502 because of its 3x3 neighborhood (lines 207-230).

Source claim: factories register class constructors by name at run time and loadable dynamic libraries provide a plugin mechanism; IO adds ImageIOFactory, ImageIO service classes and the ImageFileReader/ImageFileWriter facades, which hide format differences but not pixel type (lines 238-239, 254-334).

Source claim: streaming divides the image into requested regions; the median example requests 100x29 for a 100x25 output region because of a 2-pixel border, four stream divisions re-execute the filter four times, and iterative, Fourier/IIR, front-propagation and registration algorithms are named as not streamable (lines 352-399).

Source claim: reuse relies on OOP hierarchies, C++ templates and macros; Image<PixelType, Dimension> is the canonical template, concept checking produces early compile errors, and a 4.0 refactor replaced raw integer types with concept-named typedefs to support images over 4 GB (lines 408-465).

Source claim: maintainability practices include many small files, test-driven development at class level, KWStyle, Gerrit review, Git hooks that reject tabs/trailing whitespace, and CDash nightly/continuous builds reported to exercise about 84% of the code versus an estimated 50% industry average; the text estimates maintenance at 75% of TCO and 80% of developer activity (lines 473-542).

Source claim: the 2011 ARRA-funded refactor introduced modules, standardized integer types and typedefs for >4 GB images, migrated CVS to Git, added Gerrit and CDash@home, deprecated old compilers, extended DICOM/JPEG2000/BigTIFF/HDF5 IO, and added GPU, video, OpenCV and VXL support (lines 539-581).

Source claim: the Insight Journal requires code, data, parameters and tests, publishes within 24 hours and had received its 500th article; the authors argue that reproducibility and DIY practice improve software (lines 590-602). Inference (reader): the chapter is an author retrospective; its quantitative claims are not accompanied by measurement method or independent evaluation.

notes: Source claim: Mailman began in the early 1990s when John Viega wrote it for a Dave Matthews Band fan list; the Python community adopted it in the mid-1990s at CNRI to replace Majordomo, and Ken Manheimer contributed early work; Mark Sapiro maintains 2.1 and Barry Warsaw leads 3.0 (lines 14-17).

Source claim: two overriding principles drive message handling - no message lost and none delivered more than once - and the Mailman 2 redesign around them remained largely unchanged in Mailman 3 (lines 23-30).
Source claim: messages are modeled as a tree of MIME message objects parsed once from wire bytes, mutated as objects, pickled for persistence and flattened back to bytes at send time (lines 36-51).

Source claim: Mailman 2's MailList used cooperating mixin base classes and pickled __dict__ state in config.pck; this was convenient for adding features but exposed Python-only data, required exclusive NFS-safe locks for every read/write, and became slow, so Mailman 3 moved to SQL with Storm (SQLite default, PostgreSQL configurable) (lines 73-91).

Source claim: per-list config.pck silos prevented cross-list queries and made same-named lists in different virtual domains impossible; Mailman 3 uses the fully qualified posting address as the mailing-list primary key so support@example.com and support@example.org coexist (lines 94-100).

Source claim: parallelism comes from single-threaded runner processes, each owning a queue directory through a Switchboard; queue files are pickles with .pck/.bak/.tmp/.psv suffixes, and SHA1-based file names let power-of-2 runners split a queue without locking (lines 106-127).

Source claim: a timestamp prefix (<timestamp>+<sha1>.pck) restores best-effort FIFO ordering because SHA1 names destroy order and stat()/unpickling is avoided for performance; ordering across parallel runners is only approximate (lines 130-136).

Source claim: the master reads a configuration file, fork/execs runners, tracks PIDs and restart counts to stop restart cascades, and interprets SIGTERM/SIGINT (stop, no restart), SIGHUP (reopen logs) and SIGUSR1 (restart); it holds a lock refreshed daily by SIGALRM with a lifetime of about 1.5 days, and bin/mailman wraps start/stop/restart (lines 148-171).

Source claim: Mailman 2 mixed moderation and modification in one handler pipeline, making order significant; Mailman 3 separates chains/links/rules (rules decide and record metadata, actions dispatch) from handlers/pipelines (handlers modify and copy to digest, archive and outgoing queues) (lines 177-228).

Source claim: the default chain includes administrivia, max-size, truth and any links; deferred actions let Mailman report every rejection reason, 'any' sweeps prior matches, and 'truth' always matches at the last link to move accepted mail to the accept chain (lines 201-216).

Source claim: VERP encodes the recipient in the SMTP envelope sender (mylist-bounce+anne=example.com@example.org), so bounces return to the list; the cost is one copy per recipient instead of bundling, offset by per-recipient footers and mail-merge options (lines 234-259).

Source claim: Mailman 3 exposes a REST/JSON core engine so external UIs (the official web UI is a separate project) and scripts can integrate without the core being a bottleneck; the chapter also describes a language stack and layered templates for i18n, and closes with TDD, bytes/strings and i18n lessons plus a memorial note for Tokio Kikuchi (lines 265-329). Inference (reader): the two-tenet guarantee is argued from design, not demonstrated with fault-injection results.

notes: Source claim: matplotlib began when John Hunter tried to free epilepsy researchers from a single-license proprietary ECoG analysis package; early work was a GTK+ ECoG viewer, and a second goal was a MATLAB-like stateful plotting interface (lines 17-20).
Source claim: the architecture is three layers - backend, artist, scripting - where each upper layer knows the layer below but lower layers do not know upper ones (lines 26-29).

Source claim: the backend layer supplies FigureCanvas (surface), Renderer (drawing) and Event (input) implementations for GTK+, Qt, Tk, FLTK, wxWidgets and Cocoa, plus file backends; the agg C++ renderer gives pixel-identical screen and PNG output (lines 11, 35-50).

Source claim: everything visible is an Artist; the base class carries transform, visibility, clip box, label and picking, and its draw(renderer) call is the coupling point to a backend; primitive artists (Line2D, Rectangle, Circle, Text) compose into Axis, Tick, Axes and Figure (lines 86-107).

Source claim: Axes is the most important composite artist and holds most plotting methods; Table 11.1 maps Axes.imshow/hist/plot to AxesImage, Rectangle and Line2D instances stored on the Axes (lines 110-111).

Source claim: pyplot is a stateful thin wrapper that parses a config file for a default backend, tracks the current Figure/Axes, and forwards calls such as plot to Axes after gca(); @autogen_docstring copies API docstrings (lines 151-199).

Source claim: by version 0.98 the backend API had grown to many draw_* methods; the refactor reduced required methods to draw_path, draw_image, draw_text and get_text_width_height_descent, with draw_markers, draw_path_collection and draw_quad_mesh optional (lines 205-241).

Source claim: transforms map data to axes to figure to display through a directed graph of parent-dependent transform nodes; most are invertible, parent changes invalidate dependent nodes, affine 3x3 matrices are composed and frozen, non-affine functions handle log/polar/geographic projections, and blended nodes split x/y while shared nodes link axes (lines 246-269).

Source claim: polyline rendering is a discrete pipeline - transform, handle missing data via MOVETO, clip to figure bounds, snap horizontal/vertical lines to pixel centers for raster backends, and simplify collinear points (lines 275-285).

Source claim: math text can use a full TeX installation (parse DVI into drawing commands, usetex) or the internal mathtext engine, a TeX math-rendering port with a pyparsing parser that omits most third-party TeX/LaTeX libraries (lines 291-307).

Source claim: regression testing renders plots and compares them to baseline images using histogram RMS difference with a threshold, because FreeType variation prevents bit-exact comparison; PNG, PDF and SVG are tested, vector output is rasterized via Ghostscript/Inkscape first, and the suite takes about 15 minutes on a 2.33 GHz Core 2 E6550 with incomplete coverage (lines 313-328).

Source claim: lessons are 'Good architects borrow', the MATLAB-compatible scripting layer let the internal object API be refactored repeatedly without breaking most users, the GDK-derived drawing API was a costly borrowing mistake, and the PDF drawing specification would have been a better base; integration with Kiva/Enable was missed but integration has build and complexity costs (lines 334-340). Inference (reader): the chapter is a design history by two core authors, not an independent evaluation.

sections.title: Execution Workflow of a Web Request
Content Processing: MediaWiki Markup Language and Parser

notes: Source claim: MediaWiki is written for one site, Wikipedia, and its architecture is shaped by that constraint - top-ten traffic on a donation-funded budget, so performance, caching and optimisation are privileged, while corporate CMS features such as publication workflows and access control lists are absent and anti-vandalism tooling exists instead (lines 14-17, 26).

Source claim: three historical phases are distinguished - UseModWiki on flat files from January 2001, Manske's PHP/MySQL 'phase II' from 2001, and Crocker's 2002 'phase III' rewrite done for performance rather than design; in 2003 the developers chose further iteration over a from-scratch re-architecture (lines 54-99).

Source claim: the MediaWiki 1.5 schema change decoupled revision metadata from revision text, so an edit inserts a revision and moves a page_latest pointer and a rename no longer rewrites stored titles; external text storage blobs group roughly a dozen revisions as a full copy plus diffs, gzipped, reaching about 98% compression on Wikimedia sites (lines 144-153).

Source claim: the PHP load balancer sends all writes to one master, weights reads across slaves, drops slaves whose replication lag exceeds 30 seconds and switches the site to read-only if every slave is lagging; the 'chronology protector' stores the master's position in the user session so the writer never observes a stale read (lines 156-159).

Source claim: caching is layered - Squid/Varnish reverse proxies that are notified to purge on change, an in-memory object cache since 1.1, memcached for login sessions, a dedicated CDB-based localisation cache since 1.16, and the PHP opcode cache; a file-based page cache and a pluggable object-cache backend are offered for smaller installations (lines 189-207).

Source claim: the request path is index.php, then MediaWiki::performRequest, then initializeArticle/performAction, then finalCleanup and restInPeace, with SpecialPageFactory::executePath as the alternative branch for special pages; deferred updates are committed at the end via the job queue (lines 168-181).

Source claim: internationalisation is treated as a first-class, pervasive subsystem - UTF-8 mandated since 2005, messages held in MessagesXx.php and overridable through the MediaWiki: namespace, translation workflow at translatewiki.net with LocalisationUpdate, and the qqq (documentation) and qqx (key display) pseudo-languages (lines 225-270).

Source claim: permissions are per-action group grants configured in $wgGroupPermissions, and the authors state that MediaWiki deliberately lacks a unified permissions concept, so read or write access cannot be restricted by topic or content type without extensions (lines 276-282). Inference: this is the authors' characterisation of design intent, not an audited security property.

Source claim: wikitext has no formal specification and 'can't be represented as a formal grammar'; the parser is held stable because hundreds of millions of pages depend on its exact HTML, and the 1.12 preprocessor converts wikitext to an XML DOM that skips dead branches such as unfollowed #switch cases (lines 303-316).

Source claim: templates that accept defaulted parameters turned into a de facto functional programming language and became one of the most expensive features in performance terms, with ParserFunctions added as a stopgap; a Lua-like scripting language was under discussion (lines 327-336).

Source claim: extension registration is code execution at startup rather than cacheable data, which limits abstraction and optimisation, and skins are PHP classes that are hard to write without reinventing the wheel; the chapter's general theme is that architecture is left behind and catches up only when its cost becomes visible (lines 117, 393-402).

Representation observation: both figures are caption-only, inline links are stripped leaving parentheses with no target (lines 123, 141, 411), and the 33 headings and 2 figure captions match the live page fetched 2026-10-24.

Line 2: Checking the User Is Logged In
Line 4: Checking the User Has Permission to Use This Script

notes: Source claim: an installation is three things - code that the web server must not be able to write, a database whose tables all carry a prefix so it can be shared, and a writable moodledata directory that should sit outside the web root; load-balanced deployments share one database and one moodledata (lines 50-59).

Source claim: Moodle dispatches by direct script URL (.../course/view.php?id=123) rather than through a single front controller, and the author argues explicitly that the missing indirection layer has not hurt, while the chosen URLs stay stable across renames and moves (lines 71-77).

Source claim: contexts form a System -> category -> course -> module hierarchy, and checks use require_capability (fatal) or has_capability (boolean) against a named capability such as local/greet:begreeted (lines 213-232).

Source claim: there are four permission values - NOT SET/INHERIT, ALLOW, PREVENT and PROHIBIT - and PROHIBIT differs from PREVENT in that it cannot be overridden in sub-contexts; capabilities are declared with captype, contextlevel and archetype defaults in db/access.php (lines 246-264, 285-296).

Source claim: aggregation is PROHIBIT wins, otherwise ALLOW wins, otherwise false; the worked example assigns a system-level 'Naughty user' role with PROHIBIT to stop a user posting in every forum (lines 235-243, 299-311). Inference: the override order is deliberately non-monotonic and should not be read as deny-by-default, since PREVENT is defeatable by a lower-context ALLOW.

Source claim: request data is read through optional_param/required_param with PARAM_* cleaning, and complex forms wrap the unmaintained PEAR HTML_QuickForm library, which the author names as future migration work (lines 326-342).

Source claim: output is split between $PAGE (context, canonical URL, title, blocks, required JavaScript) and $OUTPUT (renderer); $OUTPUT cannot be initialised early because the theme depends on the context set later, so PHP magic defers it, and the theme layout is generated then split in half at the main-content div so the script can print between header and footer (lines 405-413, 479-485).

Source claim: the $OUTPUT global introduced in 2010 is described as a stepping stone, and moving view code into a plugin renderer subclass lets a theme override output completely or partially - the chapter's worked MVC refactor (lines 521-554).

Source claim: Moodle replaced ADOdb with its own thin moodle_database wrapper in 2.0; {} table placeholders, named and anonymous SQL parameters, a portable SQL subset (AS for columns but not table aliases) and compatibility helpers such as sql_concat (lines 563-617).

Source claim: schema is declared in install.xml and applied by XMLDB; foreign keys have been declared since 1.7 but are deliberately never created, because years of running without them makes inconsistent data likely and retrospective key creation infeasible (lines 623-629). Source-stated limitation, not an inference: the definitions exist without the constraints.

sections.title: Are There More Advantages to Using nginx?

notes: Source claim: the motivating case for event-driven serving is memory held per connection while a slow client drains a response - a 100 KB page over an 80 kbps link occupies a server connection for about 10 seconds, so 1,000 such clients at 1 MB each cost roughly 1 GB (lines 23-26); nginx was written in 2002 and released publicly in 2004 under a two-clause BSD licence specifically for the C10K problem, without spawning a process or thread per request (lines 38-41, 65). Inference: the memory arithmetic is an illustrative example in the chapter, not a measurement.

Source claim: the architecture is described as modular, event-driven, asynchronous, single-threaded and non-blocking; workers accept from a shared listen socket and the kernel distributes connections, so nginx itself does no arbitration between workers (lines 80-83, 104).

Source claim: process roles are one master (running as root), several unprivileged workers, a cache loader that populates shared-memory cache metadata and then exits, and a cache manager that handles expiration and is restarted by the master on failure (lines 128-154).

Source claim: the only remaining blocking case is insufficient disk throughput for a worker, mitigated by sendfile and AIO; worker counts should match cores for CPU-bound work and run 1.5-2x cores for disk-bound work (lines 107-119).

Source claim: the proxy cache is a filesystem hierarchy keyed by an MD5 of the proxy URL, with keys and metadata in shared-memory segments; responses are written to a temporary file and renamed into the cache, so temporary and cache directories should share a filesystem (lines 160-163).

Source claim: configuration has strictly non-overlapping contexts (main, http, server, upstream, location, mail), deliberately no .htaccess-style distributed configuration, a C-style syntax, and variables that are pre-compiled to indices and evaluated once per request on demand (lines 175-193).

Source claim: after the request header is read and the virtual server resolved, a request passes six phases - server rewrite, location, location rewrite (which can return the request to an earlier phase), access control, try_files and log - before a content handler produces output (lines 299-314).

Source claim: filters are ordered at compile time, operate outbound only, and no input-transformation filter mechanism exists yet; header filters decide, operate and call the next filter, and output can stream to the client before the upstream response completes (lines 320-336).

Source claim: subrequests are the chapter's highlighted mechanism - filters can issue several, results can be combined into one response, nesting is arbitrary, and this is what the SSI module and internal-redirect-style composition rely on (line 356).

Source claim: upstream modules only install callbacks (craft request, reset connection, process first response bytes, abort, finalize, trim body), and load balancing offers just round-robin and ip-hash, with failure detection and health checks described as planned work (lines 359-377).

Source claim: memory is handled by a pool allocator plus a slab allocator for shared memory, with red-black trees for cache metadata and non-regex locations; data is passed by pointer rather than memcpy, and an idle keepalive connection is said to cost 550 bytes (lines 383-392). The author also states that internals were never documented consistently, which is why third-party module development remains difficult (line 395).
Representation observation: the single architecture figure is caption-only and inline code spans are flattened; the 12 headings and 1 figure caption match the live page fetched 2026-10-24.

sections.title: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants

notes: Source claim: Open MPI was formed by the teams behind LAM/MPI, LA/MPI and FT-MPI, with the PACX-MPI team joining soon after; they chose to abandon the prior code bases and start fresh, and the first Subversion commit was on 2003-11-22 (lines 64-79).

Source claim: C was chosen over C++ because compilers lay out structs/classes differently, which would produce different on-the-wire representations; the design goals were grouped abstraction layers, run-time plugins/parameters and not letting abstraction block performance (lines 85-103).

Source claim: three layers exist - OPAL for per-process utilities and OS portability, ORTE for launching, monitoring and killing jobs across rsh/ssh and schedulers such as Torque/PBS Pro, SLURM, Oracle Grid Engine and LSF, and OMPI for the MPI API; ORTE and OMPI may bypass lower layers, and separate libraries make upward symbol use a link error (lines 109-130).

Source claim: the Modular Component Architecture places components in frameworks, one component kind per framework; v1.5 had 155 plugins and more than 40 frameworks, including third-party DSOs, and components let rival implementations expose the same API for comparison (lines 139-151).
Source claim: each framework directory holds a <framework>.h component interface, a base/ directory with discovery and open glue, and one subdirectory per component (lines 157-163).

Source claim: frameworks may be many-of-many (several network drivers active in one process), one-of-many (a single checkpoint backend), dynamic DSO-loaded, or static when compile-time binding is needed for direct calls or pre-main memory hooks (lines 166-196).

Source claim: a component struct exists once per process and generates one or more module structs; in the BTL framework the TCP component creates one module per up Ethernet interface (lines 202-205, 336).

Source claim: component structs follow mca_<framework>_<component>_component naming so the MCA core can find them with dlsym(2), and they carry framework/component version fields used for compatibility checks (lines 211-217; code at 220-245).

Source claim: per-framework and per-component structs extend the base struct by embedding it as the first member, an emulation of C++ single inheritance that permits safe upcasts but is otherwise discouraged (lines 271-327; code at 277-321).

Source claim: the TCP BTL init opens a listening socket for each up IPv4/IPv6 interface, creates a module per interface and registers each (IP, port) centrally; multiple BTL modules let a large message be fragmented round-robin across NICs for user-level channel bonding (lines 293-300, 345-351).

Source claim: developers register MCA parameters with defaults and descriptions instead of hard-coding constants; users discover them via ompi_info and set them on the command line, through environment variables, the Windows registry or INI files (lines 373-382).

Source claim: lessons are that abstraction must yield shallow call stacks and may be bypassed with hand-written assembly in hot paths, that reusable code such as libltdl should be integrated rather than rewritten, and that setup/repeated-action splits with freelists optimize the common case; the conclusion adds that one size does not fit all, disagreement is useful and people/community matter (lines 394-466). Inference (reader): this is a design retrospective by a core developer, not an independent performance evaluation.

notes: Source claim: OSCAR (Open Source Clinical Application Resource) is an approximately ten-year-old McMaster University project, a Tomcat/MySQL EMR with components such as oscarEncounter, Rx3 and the Integrator, holding CMS 3.0 certification with CMS 4.0 applied for (lines 14-23).

Source claim: the application broadly follows MVC with DAOs, servlets and JSPs separated, and data moving through request attributes, but parts predate stricter enforcement - patient creation and updates still occur in demographiccontrol.jsp (lines 32-44).

Source claim: the project moved from CVS, where broken builds and late-discovered changes were possible, to git with style checks, unit tests, compilation and code review enforced through Hudson and Gerrit (lines 53-56).

Source claim: three database-access generations coexist - DBHandler (raw JDBC/SQL), legacy Hibernate with .hbm.xml mappings, and generic JPA annotations - each integrated as it became available, with new code steered away from the older two (lines 62, 95-119).

Source claim: EForms load a template and store each instance against a patient; free-form SQL in apconfig.xml populates a POJO, DBHandler forwards unchecked SQL, so callers must prevent injection and schema changes force controller-side query edits (lines 68-83).

Source claim: Hibernate maps columns explicitly and uses prepared statements, and a startup sanity check fails fast on a bad mapping; the trade-offs are verbose per-table configuration and sometimes inefficient generated joins (lines 92-104).

Source claim: a three-table note/issue join produced a temporary table of about 7x10^12 rows, selected about 1,000, took about five minutes and locked casemgmt_note; restricting the first table in a prepared statement reduced the candidate set to 300,000 and the query to about 0.1 seconds (lines 134-146).

Source claim: the CAISI permission model assigns providers to programs and roles with global permissions checked by English phrases such as 'read doctor notes' per note; older Provider Type and Provider Roles models still coexist, and code can be dated by which model it uses (lines 155-176).

Source claim: the Integrator is a separate Tomcat/MySQL web application and near-pure web service reached by POST/GET, described by WSDL, using JPA only, with a client library in OSCAR that changes only when new functions appear (lines 182-206).

Source claim: Integrator data arrives on a schedule, only records viewed since the previous push are sent, remote charts are cached locally for one hour, and nothing is stored permanently on the Integrator; patients can revoke consent and clinics choose which data types to share (lines 212-230).

Source claim: wsdl2java generates data classes such as CachedDemographic, CachedDemographicNote and CachedProvider; OSCAR manually converts them into local classes, sets a remote-content flag for the view, and CaisiIntegratorUpdateTask performs the outbound conversion (lines 236-245).

Source claim: lessons are that poor source control produced controller/view tangles, old libraries are hard to upgrade and duplicated, adding features requires touching JSP/servlet/layout/config, documentation is missing, and DBHandler remains a security priority; the proposed redesign is plugin-modular with a third-party-audited data-access layer (lines 257-278). Inference (reader): the chapter is a maintainer's reflective case study, not an independent security audit.

sections.title: Java programs have their own threads; JavaScript can lock up your browser.
Java is strongly typed; JavaScript is not.
Java is a class/instance-based object-oriented language, with separate variable and method spaces; JavaScript is not.
Java allows method overloading; JavaScript does not.
Why Pick JavaScript if It Can't Do Java?
If All Else Fails, Tell People

notes: Source claim: Processing.js began in 2008 as John Resig's attempt to run Processing sketches on the HTML5 <canvas> without Java or plugins; the whole library is one processing.js file containing one Processing object (lines 17-23).

Source claim: the design rewrites Processing source into JavaScript and maps each API call onto the Processing object's canvas operations; separate 2D and 3D paths are bound at load time to avoid per-call mode checks (lines 23-26).

Source claim: the first parser replaced Java substrings by hand (early file lines 37-266 in the source page), broke down as the syntax set grew, and was rewritten to build an AST before emitting JavaScript, making Processing.js an on-the-fly Java-to-JavaScript transcompiler (line 32).

Source claim: the chapter lists six Java/JavaScript mismatches - program isolation, static typing, class/instance object model with separate variable and method spaces, method overloading, and compiled-code imports (lines 82-94).

Source claim: because JavaScript cannot idle, strings use synchronous XMLHttpRequest, images use Image.onload, @pjs preload directives hold sketch start until loads finish, and fonts are detected by comparing metrics against a tiny embedded 'A' font and polling (lines 106-138).

Source claim: integer division and number types are not emulated; the team deliberately left the quirk documented rather than adding a typed symbol table, judging real-world impact low (lines 144-147).

Source claim: classical inheritance is implemented on prototypes, and variables and functions still share one key space; the collision is left as a documented restriction because separating them would slow the library and break JavaScript closures (lines 153-156).
Source claim: overloads are renamed function$N by arity and dispatched with typeof and instanceof; only same-arity overloads that differ solely in numeric type remain unsupported (lines 162-165).

Source claim: compiled .jarchive imports cannot be supported without a bytecode decompiler, so a Processing.js Library API plus the import keyword was planned for 1.4; for now import is stripped from the source (lines 171-174).

Source claim: JavaScript was chosen because it is already present in browsers and, being Turing-complete, can emulate the missing Java features at a speed cost; preserving mixed Processing/JavaScript was an explicit goal that later enabled CoffeeScript use (lines 180-228).

Source claim: the single file has three logical parts - launcher (preprocess, convert, execute), static library (constants, PShape/SVG/XML, matrices, PImage, PFont caching, DrawingShared binding, ArrayList/HashMap with virtual equals/hashCode) and per-instance API code; the full object costs about 5 MB and per-sketch code about 500 KB (lines 243-338).

Source claim: development requires a unit or reference test per ticket, pixel-compares rendered output with native Processing, runs performance tests, and minifies/gzips to about 65 KB; lessons are to port for behavior rather than similarity, return early, derive tests from specifications and seek feedback early (lines 353-460). Inference (reader): the chapter is an implementer's account, not a browser benchmark study.

notes: Source claim: Puppet is a Ruby IT-management tool for datacenter automation, used from 2 to 50,000 machines; it reads a declarative specification and converges each host to it, doing nothing when already compliant, and prefers native system facilities such as yum and init.d on Red Hat and dmg and launchd on OS X (lines 14-20).

Source claim: Puppet credits CFEngine as the first general-purpose open-source configuration tool and ISconf for make-inspired explicit dependencies; resources are its primitives and must be unique per host per type and title, dependencies are first-class, and the Catalog is the resource graph that most of Puppet hangs off (lines 23-65).

Source claim: Puppet runs in client/server or serverless mode with internal network transparency; agents receive only their compiled catalog rather than raw modules, which enforces least privilege, separates the right to compile a configuration from the right to apply it, and permits disconnected operation (lines 86-89); the interchange types are Facts, Manifests, Catalogs and Reports plus files and certificates (lines 107-118).

Source claim: the External Node Classifier was added about two years after launch because classifying hosts is fundamentally different from configuring them; it returns the classes and parameters for a host and remained optional as of Puppet 2.7 (lines 139-142).

Source claim: the compiler combines a Racc-generated Yacc-style parser, a custom lexer because no open-source lexer generator existed, AST classes and a Compiler facade; manifests are lazily loaded, and the AST lets one server parse once and compile for many nodes (lines 151-160).

Source claim: compilation builds a temporary scope tree with dynamic scoping, which the author calls a long-standing nightmare, and emits a plain-data catalog; containment and dependency edges cannot coexist in SimpleGraph, so the same graph is converted between the two forms for different purposes (lines 178-187).

Source claim: the Transaction topologically sorts the graph and retrieves, compares and fixes each resource; ResourceHarness narrows the interface between Transaction and Resource; Puppet transactions deliberately lack atomicity (lines 196-219).

Source claim: the RAL is the oldest and hardest-to-change component; Puppet::Type conflates resource, resource type and type manager in under 2,000 lines; Providers separate type definition from getters and setters, enabling more than 30 package managers, and providers never decide to act, which is what makes simulation mode trustworthy (lines 225-286).

Source claim: parameters split into metaparameters, parameters and properties; reporting records events with timestamp, previous and new value, message and success, failure or simulation status, wraps them per resource in ResourceStatus, and sends metrics to the server (lines 289-301).

Source claim: plugins are downloaded at the start of every run; the Indirector is an IoC service locator exposing REST-like find, search, save and destroy, so switching from serverless to client/server is configuration rather than code; networking moved from XMLRPC to REST over two releases, JSON is replacing YAML for speed and portability, and XMLRPC is to be removed (lines 313-348).

Source claim: the lessons are that separation of language, RAL and transaction is the proudest achievement, extensibility uses the same interfaces offered to users, simplicity carries maintenance cost, configurability was taken too far, refactoring was too slow, and the language of design gave better decision criteria than the language of simplicity (lines 354-369).

Inference: the chapter explains architecture through a single-maintainer origin story (2004 prototype, Ruby chosen after a four-hour prototype); this is the author's retrospective framing and adoption or scale figures are asserted rather than measured (lines 56-77).
