notes: Source claim: PyPy is a Python implementation and a dynamic-language implementation framework, written almost entirely in Python except negligible C stubs, split into a Python interpreter written in RPython and the RPython translation toolchain (lines 11-26).

Source claim: because RPython is a strict subset, the interpreter runs untranslated on another Python implementation; this is very slow but allows fast testing and normal Python debugging, and most tests run both untranslated and translated (line 35).

Source claim: object spaces encapsulate all knowledge needed to represent and manipulate Python objects; the bytecode interpreter treats objects as black boxes and delegates, as in the BINARY_ADD example, which permits replacement representations, interception, thunking and tainting (lines 38-52); the standard objspace adds multimethod dispatch across multiple implementations per type, such as machine-word or arbitrary-precision longs, tagged pointers and string-specialised dictionaries (line 55); interp-level RPython is distinguished from app-level Python, and parts of the interpreter such as print are written app-level (line 58).

Source claim: the translator loads the RPython program, abstract-interprets it with the flow objspace into SSA flow graphs, annotates types, RTypes operations into a backend type system, optimises and hands off to the backend (lines 64-101).

Source claim: the flow objspace holds only variables and constants, constant-folds operations whose arguments are all constant, records every branch of conditional control flow, and treats modules as constants because they must be folded out (line 70).

Source claim: malloc removal flattens non-escaping allocations into scalars; the Euclidean-distance example loses two tuple mallocs and the field indirections, leaving int_sub, cast_int_to_float and direct_call operations (lines 104-161).

Source claim: inlining reduces final binary size by enabling more constant folding and malloc removal; the C backend rewrites exception handling as manual stack unwinding, inserts stack-depth checks found through call-graph cycles, and inserts garbage collection through a transformer that also adds write barriers automatically (lines 164-170).

Source claim: generated C is an intentionally ugly mess of gotos and obscure names, leaving loop optimisation and register allocation to the C compiler; collectors can be swapped by configuration and reference mistakes are avoided modulo transformer bugs (lines 170-173).

Source claim: vanilla PyPy runs up to four times slower than CPython because of objspace and multimethod indirection; the JIT is a tracing JIT generated by two hints, merge_point and can_enter_jit, after RTyping, with jitcodes serialised into the binary, a meta-interpreter that records guards, virtuals and virtualizables optimisations, blackhole bailout on guard failure and bridge retracing (lines 179-215).

Source claim: at the time of writing PyPy is a geometric average of five times faster than CPython; the JIT is not Python-specific and is used for the regular-expression engine and an experimental NumPy, and interp-level loops have been rewritten app-level for speed (lines 218-221).

Source claim: drawbacks are implicit typing, an unspecified and shifting RPython subset, whole-program translation taking about 40 minutes, extra JIT hints needed in practice, multi-layer debugging through GDB on generated C, and lowering passes that are not really independent (lines 227-239); process relies on test-driven development, CPython's regression suite, py.test, continuous integration, daily binaries and benchmarks, Mercurial branches, a fifth JIT attempt and tools such as jitviewer (lines 245-252).

Inference: the five-times and four-times figures are author-reported with no benchmark suite, hardware, warm-up or statistical method given, and the chapter describes one point in the project's history; architecture-as-accumulation, including five JIT attempts, is presented as a lesson rather than measured (lines 218-248).

notes: Source claim: SQLAlchemy is a database toolkit and ORM for Python introduced in 2005, built on the DBAPI, offering fluent complex SQL and object mapping plus a unit-of-work persistence system; it rejects database abstraction as concealment, requires the developer to consider the relational form, and calls itself a toolkit embracing leaky abstraction while automating repetitive work without removing control (lines 11-41).

Source claim: every layer is exposed as a public API split into Core, covering DBAPI interaction, SQL rendering and schema, and an ORM built on top; the explicit Core makes mapped attributes relate to Table, queries use the select construct, and rows arrive through ResultProxy, at the cost of more call-chain steps that SQLAlchemy mitigated by shortening chains, inlining and C code (lines 47-56).

Source claim: DBAPI is only a specification and varies in unicode handling, last-inserted-id retrieval, bound parameters and type behaviour; SQLAlchemy handles this with multi-level Dialect and ExecutionContext subclassing and connector mixins for multi-backend drivers such as pyodbc and zxjdbc, while Engine, Connection and ResultProxy mirror the DBAPI module, connection and cursor and a Pool procures and reuses DBAPI connections (lines 62-143).

Source claim: Table and Column are ORM-independent schema constructs collected in MetaData, following Fowler's Metadata Mapping, and dual-inherit from the schema and SQL expression packages, serving as FromClause and ColumnElement (lines 152-164).

Source claim: SQL expressions are parse trees the developer builds directly from ClauseElement nodes, inspired by SQLBuilder in Ian Bicking's SQLObject; operator overloading through ColumnOperators makes column('a') == 2 a SQL construct, and representing operators as objects rather than strings defers rendering to compilation when dialect information is known (lines 170-241).

Source claim: Compiled splits into SQLCompiler, DDLCompiler and TypeCompiler with per-dialect subclasses; visit methods recursively concatenate SQL while tracking anonymous identifiers, bound parameter names and subquery nesting, and ExecutionContext coerces the completed statement and bound values for the DBAPI (lines 247-253).

Source claim: classical mapping applies mapper() to an existing class and is called class instrumentation rather than arbitrary monkeypatching; Declarative uses a metaclass to build the Table and invoke the same mapper; version 0.4 moved SQL expression access from .c onto the mapped attributes, giving class-bound expressions and instance-bound data the same name (lines 268-325).

Source claim: InstrumentedAttribute is a descriptor delegating instance behaviour to AttributeImpl; Mapper holds MapperProperty objects whose LoaderStrategy controls deferred, eager or immediate loading and whose DependencyProcessor is chosen by relational geometry; the mapper graph is configured lazily and drives cascade, eager loading and flush ordering (lines 331-365).

Source claim: Query separates SQL rendering from data loading, traverses the mapper graph and lets each LoaderStrategy add columns and joins or produce row-population callables; loader callables introduced in 0.5 decide row handling once per query instead of per row, a large performance gain (lines 371-398).

Source claim: Session implements identity map and unit of work, evolving from a module-global thread-local objectstore.commit in 0.1 to Session in 0.2, autoflush and the transactional Session in 0.4, and expire-on-commit in 0.5; InstanceState keeps committed_state for change detection and collections subclass set, list and dict to track history (lines 404-446).

Source claim: unitofwork builds persistence commands and topologically sorts them at two levels, per-mapper buckets and then per-object batches for reference cycles, using a modified version of a cycle detector from Guido van Rossum's blog; batching reduces Python steps and DBAPI calls, and the 0.6 rewrite took weeks of design but days to implement (lines 458-491).

Inference: the chapter is a maintainer's architectural narrative; performance and maturity statements are qualitative, the 0.6 rewrite account is retrospective, and no measurements, failure data or independent review are presented (lines 398-491).

notes: Source claim: Twisted grew out of glyph's 2000 text multiplayer game Twisted Reality, whose Java implementation used three threads per connection (input, output, logic) and suffered deadlocks, corrupted caches and unreliable locking; a Python select prototype proved simpler and more reliable (lines 20-23).

Source claim: Medusa and asyncore were rejected because asyncore is such a thin socket wrapper that portability stays the programmer's problem, it was increasingly unmaintained by 2001 and its Windows support was buggy; the stated goals then were event-driven rather than threaded execution, a uniform cross-platform interface to OS event notification, batteries-included protocols, RFC conformance with a test suite, multi-protocol composition and extensibility (lines 29-54).

Source claim: the chapter contrasts single-threaded, threaded and event-driven execution (Figure 21.1) and argues the event-driven model suits many largely independent tasks that block on I/O and removes synchronization when mutable data is shared (lines 63-90); the figure image is absent locally.

Source claim: the reactor is the core event loop that knows network, file-system and timer events; the pseudo-code polls with a timeout, merges expired timers and dispatches event.process(); poll is the default, with kqueue, epoll and IOCP reactors, the last maintained by Twisted because Python does not expose IOCP (lines 108-143).

Source claim: without an abstraction each asynchronous operation must register success and error callbacks by hand, and a missing callback leaves the reactor running forever; the toy synchronous and asynchronous URL fetchers show the try/except/else/finally correspondence (lines 149-221).

Source claim: the Deferred wraps a not-yet-available result and its callback and errback chains, is fired only once (re-firing raises), and is extended with addCallbacks and addBoth; the chapter says jQuery, Dojo and MochiKit borrowed the abstraction (lines 229-275).

Source claim: transports describe stream or datagram orientation, flow control and reliability and are decoupled from protocols so many protocols reuse one transport and a mock transport can capture writes; ITransport exposes write, writeSequence, loseConnection, getPeer and getHost, while IProtocol exposes makeConnection, connectionMade, dataReceived and connectionLost, illustrated by complete echo server and client code using factories and reactor.listenTCP/connectTCP (lines 281-351); both interfaces appear locally as flattened tables.

Source claim: the application infrastructure has four parts - Services (IService startService/stopService), Applications, TAC configuration files and the twistd utility - replacing hand-written reactor start/stop, daemonization, logging and privilege handling; the sample twistd log shows Twisted 11.0.0 on Python 2.7.1 (lines 357-475). The author adds that most large Twisted deployments still rewrite parts of these management and monitoring facilities because the architecture does not expose what system administrators need (lines 540-543). Inference (reader): that last point is an anecdote, not a measured survey.

Source claim: plugins implement IPlugin and register twistd subcommands, keeping only the plugin API stable so third parties can extend the CLI; twisted.cred plugs authentication into the same mechanism, and shipped plugins include web, dns, conch and mail (lines 481-537).

Source claim: TAP stored configuration and state as pickles, broke when classes changed, and required a matrix of upgraders; it was removed in favour of TAC files and plugins, with the lesson that persistent data needs an explicit schema (lines 555-577).

Source claim: the web2 rewrite was labelled experimental, was used by major projects and accidentally packaged by Debian, coexisted with twisted.web for years and was removed in 2011; the author says incremental backwards-compatible changes and deprecations would have been better (lines 583-598).

Source claim: maintaining many protocols is bounded by volunteer time - HTTP/1.1 support took 2005-2009 for a 1999 RFC, IPv6 was still unmerged in 2011, and Wokkel and WebSockets stayed outside core - while a strict test-driven policy and coding standards protect compatibility (lines 604-616).

notes: Source claim: Yesod is a Haskell web framework that exploits static typing for safety and speed; the author argues the static/dynamic language dichotomy is false, that Haskell eliminates null-pointer exceptions and favours immutable data, and that its compiler catches more bugs than Java-style typing. Yesod resembles Rails and Django in following MVC, separating templates from logic, providing an ORM and using front-controller routing, but pushes error detection into compilation and uses Template Haskell to automate type-safe-URL boilerplate (lines 20-45).

Source claim: WAI exists because baking a server into a framework limits deployment options; it targets generality and performance, models an application as Request -> Response, keeps binary ByteString and textual Text separate, and stores raw query bytes plus parsed values (lines 51-73).

Source claim: a plain ByteString cannot hold whole request or response bodies at scale, so WAI uses enumerators (similar to Python generators) and an Application becomes Request -> Iteratee ByteString IO Response; builders then describe how to fill buffers, minimising system calls and copies, with blaze-builder tuned experimentally and headers prepended to the body (lines 79-107).

Source claim: handlers run WAI applications and include Warp, FastCGI, SCGI, CGI, Webkit, Launch and a test handler; Warp uses one GHC green thread per connection and GHC's asynchronous I/O over kqueue, epoll or select, giving event-driven performance without callbacks, and the chapter cites the PONG benchmark where Warp, Happstack and Snap lead (lines 113-134); both figures are absent locally.

Source claim: middleware is an application transformer (Application -> Application) such as gzip, jsonp, autohead and debug, stackable by modifying the request on the way in and the response on the way out; wai-test supplies mock requests and response assertions but does not remove the need for testing (lines 140-176).

Source claim: Yesod's Shakespearean template languages occupy a middle ground between arbitrary embedded code and argument-only templates; Hamlet, Julius, Cassius and Lucius are checked at compile time for well-formedness, variable resolution and type safety, and CSS/JavaScript compile into the executable with builder-based rendering (lines 182-197 and 274-289).

Source claim: interpolated Hamlet content must have type Html, so Text cannot be inserted directly; toHtml escapes entities (the script-tag example) while preEscapedText inserts verbatim to avoid double escaping, and toHtml is the default; type-safe URLs represent routes as a datatype such as FibRoute and are rendered to text by a function (lines 203-271).

Source claim: Persistent is backend-agnostic and fully type-checked, with escape hatches for backend-specific features and raw queries; PersistValue, PersistField, PersistEntity and PersistBackend compose the model, and a Person entity maps Text/Day/PNG fields to SQL VARCHAR/Date/BLOB or MongoDB fields (lines 295-330); the mapping table is flattened locally.

Source claim: every Persistent interaction is typed, so changing an entity declaration makes the compiler find affected code, which the author argues is stronger than test coverage; Persistent generates SQL schema, applies per-backend migrations (ALTER TABLE on PostgreSQL, table copy on SQLite, none on MongoDB), refuses destructive changes and reports unsafe operations, and typed IDs such as PersonId support relations (lines 335-397).

Source claim: Yesod's core contribution is declarative routing with explicit request methods, typed path parameters such as EntryId that are marshalled automatically (404 on parse failure), and type-safe URL values that eliminate malformed links; handlers are named methodResourceR, run in a Handler monad and return a HasReps value so one resource can serve HTML or JSON by Accept header (lines 403-515).

Source claim: widgets bundle HTML, CSS and JavaScript with their dependencies and can run handler code, then defaultLayout assembles the page; assets are either inlined or emitted as content-hashed external files for far-future caching, with JavaScript loaded asynchronously through yepnope.js, and subsites such as static files and authentication are added with one route line and reuse the site layout (lines 521-581).

Source claim: the lessons are that the delivered system diverges from the initial goal list, that lack of mastery should not block starting, and that project approachability, documented standards and automated build tooling matter when a single-author project becomes a team effort (lines 587-605). Inference (reader): the chapter is a framework author's design rationale, not a comparative benchmark study.

sections.title: 23.1. Introduction to the Poky Build System

notes: Source claim: the Yocto Project gives embedded Linux developers a hardware-agnostic starting point of tools, processes, templates and methods; its core is the Poky build system, and the chapter focuses on BitBake, a Gentoo-Portage-inspired metadata-driven build tool shared by Yocto and OpenEmbedded (line 11).

Source claim: the lineage runs from the 2001 Sharp Zaurus and OpenZaurus on buildroot, through 2003 discussions that became OpenEmbedded (Larson, Lauer, Schurig), to Richard Purdie's Poky as a stabilized OpenEmbedded branch, and the November 2010 Linux Foundation announcement that created the Yocto Project and OE-Core coordination (lines 14-17).

Source claim: Poky release 1.1 'edison' can produce images from a minimal shell image to an LSB-compliant image with the Sato GMAE interface; layers add BSPs, software stacks or image types, and oe-init-build-env sets up the shell, generates configuration and checks prerequisites including Pseudo, a fakeroot replacement (lines 23-29).

Source claim: BitBake parses configuration, layers, classes and recipes, builds a weighted dependency chain so that tasks needed by the most other tasks run earlier, re-parses only changed metadata, then executes the queue across threads limited by BB_NUMBER_THREADS; the default task order is fetch, unpack, configure, cross-compile, split into packages, package as rpm/ipk/deb and assemble the root filesystem (lines 32-35).

Source claim: every aspect of a Poky build is controlled by metadata, either configuration files or non-executable recipes that declare description, version, license, upstream source, inherited build classes and extra or prepended/appended tasks; configuration splits into BitBake-wide files and per-layer files, with meta-yocto itself a layer over OE-Core's meta layer (lines 41-44).

Source claim: the worked layering example builds a Crownbay NAS with x32 by combining a Crownbay BSP layer, meta-x32, meta-baryon and an imaginary meta-myproject GUI layer; BBLAYERS in bblayers.conf lists them, and each layer's conf/layer.conf extends BBPATH and BBFILES and sets a collection name and priority (lines 47-93).

Source claim: BBCooker starts the build, parseConfigurationFiles reads bblayers.conf, then each layer.conf, then bitbake.conf for global variables and includes such as local.conf and machine configuration; the grep recipe shows LICENSE with LIC_FILES_CHKSUM, SRC_URI md5 and sha256 checksums, autotools/gettext inheritance, install-time renames and update-alternatives hooks (lines 98-168).

Source claim: BitBake 1.0 kept every recipe variable in one large dictionary, had no data cache or shared state, could not build incrementally, retried failed tasks later and restarted builds from scratch; version 1.13.3 adds a client-server architecture, a datastore, copy-on-write storage, shared state and much better dependency computation (lines 176-179).

Source claim: all builds start a user-interface instance (knotty by default, Hob as the graphical interface), which sends commands to a server (process server by default, XMLRPC also supported), which brings up the cooker; the cooker parses metadata, creates the runqueue and triggers the build, while the command module executes commands and emits events to the UI (lines 185-194).

Source claim: DataSmart uses Tom Ansell's copy-on-write dictionary so shared global variables are stored once and each recipe layer stores only its diff; lookups walk down the COW stack, and variables containing Python are validated with bb.codeparser for syntax and circular references, illustrated by the LIBCEXTENSION expression (lines 200-218).

Source claim: BitBake distinguishes build-time DEPENDS from runtime RDEPENDS and recognises internally dependent, DEPENDS-dependent, RDEPENDS-dependent and inter-task task dependencies; provider selection honours PREFERRED_PROVIDER and weights versions and dependents, then TaskData is converted into a weighted runqueue; the chapter reports three to four hours single-threaded versus 30-40 minutes with 14 threads and PARALLEL_MAKE -j 12 for core-image-minimal in 2011 (lines 224-280).

Source claim: the conclusion urges a written, flexible standards document (the inconsistent LICENSE values are the example), heavy front-end planning and modular design, and notes that earlier datastore planning might have avoided the low-memory problems; the acknowledgements credit BitBake, OpenEmbedded, OE-Core and Yocto contributors (lines 286-316). Inference (reader): the timing comparison is one machine and one image, not a controlled benchmark.

Code indentation is collapsed inside the extractor's [CODE]/[/CODE] markers (the AMQP example's four-space continuations appear as one space), and 224 separator lines carry spaces only. No table. No prose section is missing relative to the live headings.
notes: Source claim: ØMQ is a messaging system or message-oriented middleware used in financial services, game development, embedded systems, academic research and aerospace; it began as ultra-fast messaging for stock trading, spent its first year on benchmarking methodology, its second on generic distributed applications and its third on usability and the BSD Sockets API, while standardisation and an experimental in-kernel implementation are explicitly out of scope (lines 11-32).

Source claim: a broker puts every message through the network twice and eventually becomes the bottleneck, while organisational boundaries make one central messaging server untenable; ØMQ therefore chose a 'smart endpoint, dumb network' library based on the end-to-end principle, which the author reports as both faster and more flexible, with the operational benefit that no messaging server has to be installed or administered (lines 38-56).

Source claim: global variables in a library break when it is instantiated twice in one process, so ØMQ has none; the user creates an explicit context object to hold global state, which from the user's side behaves like a pool of worker threads, and each library instance can have its own context (lines 62-71; Figure 24.1 is caption-only).

Source claim: latency and throughput are not inverses; the worked example sends five messages over six seconds, giving a naive 1.2 s 'latency' although individual message latencies are 2-4 s, and throughput differs at sender (2.5 msgs/s) and receiver (1.25 msgs/s); latency exists only between two points per message, throughput only at one point over a set of messages, and their relation belongs to queueing theory (lines 77-101).

Source claim: optimisation should target the critical path, and for ØMQ the critical factors are memory allocations, system calls and the concurrency model; connection setup and error handling are rare and therefore negligible, and small messages cost one allocation per 256 messages, dropping to zero under a steady stream because chunks are reused (lines 110-131).

Source claim: small messages are encoded directly in an opaque handle so copying the handle copies the data, while large messages live in a separate reference-counted buffer reached by a pointer so copying the handle does not copy the payload; the author presents this as zero-copy for large messages and a deliberate split between allocation and copy cost (lines 137-146).

Source claim: batching avoids repeated traversal of the whole network stack and can improve throughput by up to two orders of magnitude, but adds latency, as Nagle's algorithm and NIC interrupt coalescing show; ØMQ disables lower-layer batching when traffic is sparse, batches aggressively at the topmost layer only once queues build, and turns batching off again when the queue empties (lines 152-182).

Source claim: a socket lives in the user's thread while worker threads own asynchronous objects in a tree with one owner per object; listeners and connectors create session/engine pairs, the single session type talks to the socket while per-protocol engines (TCP, IPC, PGM) talk to the network, two pipe objects per session carry messages in each direction as lock-free queues, and a context holds global state (lines 191-209).

Source claim: ØMQ adopted the actor model to scale across cores: one worker thread per core, each object bound to one thread with no migration, no mutexes or semaphores, and fully asynchronous event-driven state machines under a cooperative scheduler; clean shutdown of these state machines is the hardest subsystem, with the author reporting that roughly 30-50% of bug-tracker issues relate to shutdown (lines 215-236).

Source claim: pipe queues have exactly one writer and one reader, so 1-to-N communication uses multiple queues and no writer/writer or reader/reader synchronisation is needed; atomics are still expensive, so writers accumulate messages in a pre-write area and flush with one atomic pointer change, and readers shift the queue into a pre-read area with another single atomic operation (lines 242-261).

Source claim: the API moved from AMQP's exchange/queue model to the BSD Sockets API at the end of 2009, after which adoption reportedly rose tenfold and some 20 language bindings appeared; the author argues that reusing a decades-old, widely known API flattens the learning curve and lets ØMQ share event loops and conceptual infrastructure (lines 269-290).

Source claim: ØMQ rejects a generic routing system such as AMQP in favour of small orthogonal messaging patterns (publish/subscribe, request/reply, pipeline), implemented as a scalability layer over transports analogous to TCP/UDP/SCTP/DCCP; the AMQP RPC client takes 13 lines against four for a ØMQ REQ socket, and the conclusion frames distributed computing as an everyday problem whose solutions remain mostly domain-specific hacks (lines 299-375). Inference (reader): the performance, adoption and bug-share numbers are author-reported, not measured or independently verified here.

Candidate context for where latency and throughput are measured; the five-message example and the rule that latency is between two points while throughput is at one point are the concrete case.
Candidate context for benchmark design and confounders; the first year spent on benchmarking methodology and the critique of dividing total time by message count are the concrete case.

Candidate context for actor-style coordination and thread affinity; one worker thread per core, non-migrating objects, cooperative scheduling and the shutdown-bug share are the concrete case, though the page addresses cancellation and resource ownership.

Candidate context for API surface as a product boundary; replacing the AMQP exchange/queue API with BSD sockets and the resulting adoption change are the concrete case, though the page addresses HTTP/RPC contracts.
Candidate context for orthogonal layer implementations and stable boundaries; the scalability layer with non-intersecting messaging patterns over pluggable transport engines is the concrete case.

readings.revision: official documentation, page captured 2026-10-24
readings.coverage: Registered page only, not the whole documentation site: local capture of the Cassandra 'Architecture Overview' page, lines 1-74 (638 words), read sequentially and completely, including the untitled introduction, Features and Operating sections. Extractor preamble (Title, URL Source, Published Time, 'Markdown Content:') retained; site navigation, footer, cookie/consent chrome and all other documentation pages excluded and not read.

notes: Source claim (lines 8-12): Cassandra is presented as an open-source, distributed NoSQL database implementing a partitioned wide-column storage model with eventually consistent semantics; it was initially designed at Facebook using a staged event-driven architecture and combines Dynamo-style distribution and replication with a Bigtable-style data and storage engine model.

Source claim (lines 14-28): the page lists seven design objectives: full multi-primary database replication; global availability at low latency; scaling out on commodity hardware; linear throughput increase with each additional processor; online load balancing and cluster growth; partitioned key-oriented queries; and flexible schema.

Source claim (lines 32-42): CQL organizes data as keyspace (replication strategy across datacenters, container for tables) -> table (rows and columns, partitioned by the partition key, new columns addable with zero downtime) -> partition (the mandatory part of the primary key identifying the node that stores the row) -> row (partition key plus optional clustering keys) -> column (a typed single datum).

sections.heading: Introduction: column-oriented storage and vectorized query execution (untitled)

notes: Source claim (line 6): ClickHouse is described as a true column-oriented DBMS that stores data by columns and dispatches operations on arrays ('vectorized query execution'); the page traces array programming to APL and VectorWise, contrasts vectorization with runtime code generation, and states that ClickHouse uses vectorized execution with limited initial runtime code-generation support.

Source claim (lines 8-10): `IColumn` represents in-memory column chunks; almost all operations are immutable (filter for WHERE/HAVING, permute for ORDER BY, cut for LIMIT); concrete layouts are usually contiguous arrays, while String and Array columns use two vectors (values plus offsets); `ColumnConst` stores one value but looks like a column.

Source claim (lines 12-18): `Field` is a discriminated union of UInt64, Int64, Float64, String and Array, and per-value access via `operator[]`/`insert` is slower than bulk methods; 'leaky abstractions' let specialized routines cast to a concrete `IColumn` and read or fill its internal array directly (for example `ColumnUInt64::getData`), and `Field` loses type width because UInt8..UInt64 all appear as UInt64.

Source claim (lines 20-26): `IDataType` owns serialization/deserialization in binary and text and stores only metadata; it is loosely coupled to `IColumn` (DataTypeUInt32 and DataTypeDateTime both use ColumnUInt32, and DataTypeUInt8 may use ColumnUInt8 or ColumnConstUInt8). A `Block` is a set of (IColumn, IDataType, column name) triples; function results are appended as new columns, unneeded columns are removed rather than modified, and blocks are created per processed chunk.

Source claim (lines 40-49): `IStorage` represents tables, with engines such as StorageMergeTree and StorageMemory; `read` takes columns, the AST and a desired stream count and returns a `Pipe` of Processors; `QueryProcessingStage` reports which parts of the query the storage already computed; `StorageDistributed` may preprocess remotely, and `TableFunction`s return a temporary `IStorage` for a FROM clause.

Source claim (lines 51-59): a hand-written recursive-descent parser builds an AST (parser generators are not used 'for historical reasons'); interpreters turn the AST into a QueryPipeline - pulling for SELECT, pushing for INSERT, completed for INSERT SELECT. The page states that `InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer` with `QueryTree` has been the default since 24.3, the only analysis option since 26.9 (when `enable_analyzer` became obsolete and frozen at 1), and the only analyzer since 26.10; ExpressionAnalyzer remains for standalone expressions such as TTL, sharding keys, defaults and projections.

Source claim (lines 61-69): ordinary functions keep row counts and run on Blocks rather than individual rows, so they are not short-circuited; strong typing means functions must explicitly support each type combination (for example `plus` is template-instantiated across numeric type pairs). Aggregate functions are stateful through `IAggregateFunction`, states live in an `Arena` memory pool for high-cardinality GROUP BY, can be serialized for distributed execution or disk spill, and their serialized format is not versioned, with backward compatibility required because `AggregatingMergeTree` is used in production.

Source claim (lines 81-101): configuration uses Poco `AbstractConfiguration`, is merged from XML/YAML files by `ConfigProcessor`, and can be reloaded by `ConfigReloader` or `SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG`; settings form a context hierarchy (global, session, query, background) merged in six ordered steps from global defaults through query SETTINGS, with later sources overriding earlier ones.

Source claim (lines 103-135): work runs on several thread pools (server, global, IO, background schedule, preemptable) built on the global pool with priority queues; `ConcurrencyControl` introduces CPU 'slots' limited by `concurrent_threads_soft_limit_num`, with free/granted/acquired states, `allocate(1, max_threads)` guaranteeing at least one slot per query, and runtime adjustment of the limit.

Source claim (lines 137-139): a `Distributed` table stores no data and acts as a view over local tables; SELECT is rewritten, remote nodes process only to a mergeable stage, and results are merged. The page states there is no global query plan - each node has a local plan for its part - and that reshuffling data between servers for high-cardinality GROUP BY or large JOINs is not supported and remains future work.

Source claim (lines 141-147): MergeTree parts are immutable, ordered by primary key, with a sparse `primary.idx` (one key per `index_granularity`, usually 8192 rows) and `column.mrk` marks; background merges reduce part count and cause write amplification; MergeTree is explicitly not an LSM tree because it has no memtable or log. Replication is per-table via `ReplicatedMergeTree` and a ZooKeeper path, asynchronous multi-master and conflict-free because ClickHouse does not support UPDATEs; inserts are not quorum-acknowledged by default (data can be lost on node failure) unless `insert_quorum` is enabled, and replication is physical (compressed parts, not queries).

Coverage and representation note: 'Processors' (lines 28-30) and 'Formats' (lines 32-34) are one-line pointers to `IProcessor.h` in the published page, not omissions of this capture; five long lines exceeded the read tool's display cap and were re-read verbatim from the local file; headings are plain text with no navigation or footer chrome. sections.heading: What is it Made Up Of?
Logic Half in Client, Half in Server
Servers are Disconnected From Each Other

notes: Source claim (lines 6-10): memcached is described as a free and open-source, high-performance, distributed memory object caching system, generic in nature but intended to speed up dynamic web applications by alleviating database load; it is an in-memory key-value store for small arbitrary data (strings, objects) produced by database calls, API calls or page rendering, with a simple design and client APIs for most popular languages.

Source claim (lines 14-18): the page frames memcached as a developer tool, explicitly 'not a code accelerator, nor database middleware', and redirects readers who are installing an application to that application's documentation; it links a separate tutorial for core concepts.

Source claim (lines 20-25): the system is composed of client software given a list of available servers, a client-based hashing algorithm that chooses a server from the key, server software that stores values with their keys in an internal hash table, and LRU logic that decides when to evict old data or reuse memory when out of memory.

Source claim (lines 31-33): the server does not care what the data looks like; items consist of a key, an expiration time, optional flags and raw data, and the server does not understand data structures, so values must be pre-serialized; some commands (incr/decr) may operate on the underlying data in a simple manner.

Source claim (lines 35-39): responsibility is split - clients understand which server to read from or write to for an item and what to do when a server cannot be contacted, while servers store and fetch items and manage when to evict or reuse memory.

Source claim (lines 41-43): servers are unaware of each other - no crosstalk, synchronization, broadcasting or replication; adding servers increases available memory, and cache invalidation is simplified because clients delete or overwrite data directly on the server that owns it.

Source claim (lines 45-49): all commands are implemented to be as fast and lock-friendly as possible for near-deterministic query speeds; the page asserts that queries on slow machines should run well under 1 ms and that high-end servers can serve millions of keys per second.

Source claim (lines 51-57): memcached is by default a least-recently-used cache with per-item expiration; the page presents expiration and eviction as deliberate features for limiting stale data or retaining frequently requested information, states there are no garbage-collector pauses and that free space is lazily reclaimed, and links an external new_lru.txt document for the latest algorithm.

Inference (reader, not stated on the page): because servers neither replicate nor synchronize and items expire or are evicted, the page positions memcached as a non-authoritative, loss-tolerant cache; it states no durability, replication or consistency guarantee, and any such guarantee would be an over-read.

Inference (reader): client-side hashing plus a server list implies that changing cluster membership changes the key-to-server mapping and can invalidate many entries at once; the page does not discuss consistent hashing or resharding behavior, so that topic is outside this page.

Scope note: the page explicitly defers detail to external material (memcached.org/about, the tutorial, and new_lru.txt for LRU); those references are recorded in omissions and were not read for this record.

sections.heading: API v1 saved-response replay versus API v2 retry-to-completion
Client key generation, entropy and 255-character limit
API v1 key removal, reuse after pruning and parameter matching
API v1 save boundary after endpoint execution begins
API v1 method scope: POST, GET and DELETE

notes: Source claim (L4): the API supports idempotency so that requests can be retried safely without performing the same operation twice; when creating or updating an object an idempotency key lets a connection error be retried without creating a second object or repeating the update.
Source claim (L6): an idempotent request adds an IdempotencyKey element to the request options.

Source claim (L8): for API v1 Stripe saves the status code and body of the first request made with a given key once endpoint execution begins; retries with the same key return the saved response, including 500 errors. For API v2, retries do not repeat successful operations; failed or partially failed work is retried to completion where possible, an updated response is returned, and if a retry cannot succeed an error explains why.

Source claim (L10): the client generates the key. V4 UUIDs or another random string with sufficient entropy are suggested to avoid collisions; keys are up to 255 characters; sensitive data such as email addresses or personal identifiers should not be used as keys.

Source claim (L12): for API v1, keys can be removed from the system automatically once they are at least 24 hours old; reuse after the original is pruned generates a new request; the idempotency layer compares incoming parameters with the original request and errors on mismatch to prevent accidental misuse.

Source claim (L14): for API v1 results are saved only after endpoint execution begins. Requests failing parameter validation, or conflicting with a concurrently executing request, store no idempotent result because no endpoint execution starts, and they may be retried.
Source claim (L16): for API v1 all POST requests accept idempotency keys; keys on GET and DELETE have no effect because those methods are idempotent by definition.

Source claim (L19-L21): the retained example is a customer-create POST with header Idempotency-Key: KG5LxwFBepaKHyUD; the capture flattens the shell line continuations and shows a redacted placeholder secret key.

Definition and contrast with physical replication (L8)
Publish/subscribe model, subscribers, publications and cascading re-publication (L10)
Initial snapshot, continuous change stream, ordering and transactional consistency (L12)

notes: Source claim (L8): logical replication replicates data objects and their changes based on their replication identity, usually a primary key, in contrast to physical replication's exact block addresses and byte-by-byte copying; PostgreSQL supports both concurrently and logical replication permits fine-grained control over data replication and security.

Source claim (L10): logical replication uses a publish-and-subscribe model with one or more subscribers subscribing to one or more publications on a publisher node; subscribers pull data and may re-publish it for cascading replication or more complex configurations.

Source claim (L12): replication typically starts by taking a snapshot of table data on the publisher database and copying it to the subscriber; changes since the initial copy are then sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, with transactional consistency guaranteed for publications within a single subscription. The text calls this transactional replication.

Source claim (L16-28): cited use cases are sending incremental changes in a database or subset, firing triggers per change on the subscriber, consolidating multiple databases (for example for analytics), replicating across major versions, replicating across platforms (Linux to Windows example), giving different user groups access, and sharing a database subset among databases.

Source claim (L30): the subscriber behaves like any other PostgreSQL instance and can itself publish; a subscriber treated as read-only by an application yields no conflicts from a single subscription, but other writes by an application or other subscribers to the same tables can create conflicts.

Inference: this is a conceptual chapter overview. Operational detail on publications, subscriptions, slots, failover, row filters, column lists, generated columns, conflicts, restrictions, architecture, monitoring, security, configuration and upgrades lives in the fourteen subpages and is not in this unit.

Inference: the transactional-consistency guarantee is explicitly qualified to publications within a single subscription, so it does not imply global ordering across subscriptions or freedom from write conflicts.

Representation note: the live PostgreSQL 18 page matches the captured prose at L8-30 and adds a Table of Contents for 29.1-29.14 that the local markdown lacks; the chapter therefore remains partial even though no landing-page prose gap was detected.

Inference: the phrase 'When logical replication of a table typically starts' describes a usual initial-sync path rather than a universal guarantee for every table state; the details are deferred to subpages.

29.9 Architecture: walsender logical decoding, pgoutput plugin, conversion to the logical replication protocol, publication filtering, transfer to the apply worker (L8)
Apply-process role: session_replication_role=replica, triggers and rules disabled by default, per-table ENABLE TRIGGER / ENABLE RULE (L10)
Trigger scope: apply fires row triggers only, not statement triggers; initial synchronization acts like COPY and fires row and statement triggers for INSERT (L12)
29.9.1 Initial Snapshot: parallel per-table synchronization workers, one replication slot each, copy visibility, catch-up streaming in publisher order, handback to the main apply process (L16)
Note: the publish parameter affects DML replication only and does not filter the initial data copy (L18-20)
Note: a failed table synchronization worker is detected and respawned; wal_retrieve_retry_interval is cited (L22-24)
notes: Source claim (L8): logical replication has an architecture similar to physical streaming replication and is implemented by walsender and apply processes; walsender starts logical decoding of the WAL and loads the pgoutput plugin, which converts WAL changes to the logical replication protocol and filters data by the publication specification; data is streamed to the apply worker, which maps it to local tables and applies changes in correct transactional order.

Source claim (L10): the subscriber apply process always runs with session_replication_role set to replica, so triggers and rules do not fire by default; users may enable them per table with ALTER TABLE and the ENABLE TRIGGER and ENABLE RULE clauses.

Source claim (L12): the apply process currently fires row triggers only, not statement triggers; initial table synchronization is implemented like COPY and therefore fires both row and statement triggers for INSERT.

Source claim (L16): initial data is snapshotted and copied by parallel instances of a special apply process, dedicated table synchronization workers spawned per table; each creates its own replication slot, copied contents become visible to other backends when the copy finishes, the worker then streams changes that occurred during the copy, applies and commits them in publisher order, and returns control to the main apply process.
Source claim (L20): the publication publish parameter affects only which DML operations are replicated; initial data synchronization does not take it into account when copying existing table data.

Source claim (L24): if a table synchronization worker fails during copy, the apply worker detects the failure and respawns it so transient errors do not permanently disrupt the setup; the text points to wal_retrieve_retry_interval.

Inference: one replication slot and one synchronization worker per table mean capacity demand tracks the number of tables being synchronized, not only the number of subscriptions; this is consistent with the reserve for table synchronization described in Section 29.12.

Inference: trigger behavior differs by phase. Initial COPY fires row and statement INSERT triggers, while streaming apply fires row triggers only; the page does not state whether triggers enabled on the subscriber fire during the catch-up streaming phase.
Inference: 'correct transactional order' describes apply order of streamed changes; the page makes no claim of global ordering across subscriptions or of DDL replication.

Column-list definition, subscriber superset requirement and default of all columns (L8)
Motivation and security caveat: behavioral or performance choice, not a security boundary; malicious subscriber can obtain unpublished columns; publisher-side protections (L10)

Column list with FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA is not supported (L18)
Partitioned tables: publish_via_partition_root selects the root or per-partition column list (L20)
Replica identity columns required for UPDATE/DELETE publications; may be omitted for INSERT-only (L22)
Initial synchronization copies published columns only, with pre-15 and pre-18 subscriber exceptions (L26)

Warning: no support for different column lists for the same table across several publications; creation is blocked but later publication changes can break apply, with matching-and-recreate remedies (L28-34)
29.5.1 Examples: table and publication DDL, \dRp+ and \d inspection, subscriber-side subset table, inserts and observed replicated rows (L36-101)
notes: Source claim (L8): each publication can optionally specify which columns of each table are replicated; the subscriber table must have at least all published columns; with no column list all publisher columns are replicated; CREATE PUBLICATION documents the syntax.

Source claim (L10): column choice may be based on behavioral or performance reasons, but must not be relied on for security because a malicious subscriber is able to obtain data from columns that are not specifically published; protections can be applied at the publisher side.
Source claim (L12): with no column list, columns added to the table later are automatically replicated, so a column list naming all columns is not the same as having no column list.
Source claim (L14): a column list can contain only simple column references and the order of columns is not preserved; the example publishes (id, b, a, d) and subsequently displays (id, a, b, d).

Source claim (L16): generated columns can be specified in a column list, allowing them to be published regardless of the publish_generated_columns publication parameter; Section 29.6 covers the details.
Source claim (L18): specifying a column list when the publication also publishes FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA is not supported.
Source claim (L20): for partitioned tables, publish_via_partition_root determines the list; true uses the root partitioned table's list, false (the default) uses each partition's list.
Source claim (L22): if a publication publishes UPDATE or DELETE, any column list must include the table's replica identity columns; an INSERT-only publication may omit them.
Source claim (L24): column lists have no effect for the TRUNCATE command.

Source claim (L26): initial synchronization copies only published columns, but subscribers before release 15 copy all columns ignoring lists, and subscribers before release 18 do not copy generated columns even when they are defined on the publisher.

Source claim (L28-34): subscriptions combining several publications where the same table has different column lists are unsupported; CREATE SUBSCRIPTION disallows creating them, but publication-side additions or alterations after subscription creation can produce the situation and cause subscriber errors; the stated remedy is to make the lists match and then recreate the subscription or use ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... DROP PUBLICATION and re-add.

Inference: the feature is a name-based projection, not a security control and not a stable schema contract; without a list, later column additions are silently included, while an explicit list must be maintained as the table evolves. No measurements or experiments are reported on this page.

notes: Source claim (L40): logical replication requires several configuration options, and these options are relevant only on one side of the replication.

Source claim (L56): on the subscriber, max_active_replication_origins must be at least the number of subscriptions that will be added plus some reserve for table synchronization.

Source claim (L60): max_worker_processes may need to be adjusted to at least max_logical_replication_workers + 1, and extensions and parallel queries also take worker slots from it.
Source claim (L62): max_sync_workers_per_subscription controls the parallelism of the initial data copy at subscription initialization or when new tables are added.

sections: Extractor metadata: title, URL, published time and 'Markdown Content:' label (L1-7; excluded)
Conflict definition: data is updated even if changed locally; an incoming constraint violation stops replication; missing rows for UPDATE/DELETE are conflicts that are skipped without error (L8)
Logged conflict cases and statistics: insert_exists, update_origin_differs, update_exists, update_missing, delete_origin_differs, delete_missing, multiple_unique_conflicts (L10-31)
Other conflict scenarios such as exclusion-constraint violations without additional log detail (L33)
Log format: LOG line with relation and conflict type; DETAIL explanation and detail_values grammar (L35-46)

LOG and DETAIL semantics: relation and conflict type; origin, transaction ID and commit timestamp; Key, existing local row, remote row and replica identity; column-name visibility and 64-byte value truncation (L48-72)
Privileges and row-level security as conflict sources (L74)
Error conflicts stop replication and require manual resolution (L76-78)
Worked ERROR log example with unique key, local/remote rows, origin name and finish LSN (L80-83)
Skip procedure: ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP or pg_replication_origin_advance(), with the inconsistency risk of skipping a whole transaction (L85)
Parallel streaming caveat: finish LSN may be unlogged; switch streaming mode to reproduce the conflict (L87)
notes: Source claim (L8): logical replication behaves like normal DML in that data is updated even if it was changed locally; if incoming data violates constraints, replication stops and this is called a conflict; for UPDATE or DELETE, missing data is also a conflict but is not an error and the operation is skipped.

Source claim (L10-31): seven conflict cases are logged and counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats: insert_exists, update_origin_differs, update_exists, update_missing, delete_origin_differs, delete_missing and multiple_unique_conflicts.

Source claim (L12-31): insert_exists, update_exists and multiple_unique_conflicts violate NOT DEFERRABLE unique constraints and raise errors until resolved manually; their origin and commit-timestamp details require track_commit_timestamp on the subscriber; update_origin_differs and delete_origin_differs can only be detected with that setting, and the update or delete is always applied regardless of the local row's origin; update_missing and delete_missing are skipped.
Source claim (L19): updating a partitioned table can move a row into another partition, where a NOT DEFERRABLE unique constraint may then produce an insert_exists conflict.
Source claim (L33): exclusion-constraint violations and other scenarios exist but currently receive no additional detail in the log.

Source claim (L35-46): the log format is 'LOG: conflict detected on relation "schemaname.tablename": conflict=conflict_type' plus 'DETAIL: detailed_explanation. {detail_values}', where detail values are Key, existing local row, remote row, or replica identity (including full).

Source claim (L48-72): DETAIL includes origin, transaction ID and commit timestamp when available; Key values are given for unique-constraint conflicts; existing local and remote rows are included per conflict type; remote unchanged toasted values appear as null; replica identity shows the lookup key; column names appear only when the user lacks access to all columns; large values are truncated to 64 bytes; multiple_unique_conflicts emits one explanation per constraint.

Source claim (L74): logical replication runs with the subscription owner's privileges; permission failures on target tables cause conflicts, as does enabled row-level security the owner is subject to, regardless of whether a policy would reject the operation; the RLS restriction may be lifted in a future version.

Source claim (L76-85): an error-producing conflict stops replication and must be resolved manually; resolution is by changing subscriber data or permissions, or by skipping the transaction with ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP using the finish LSN, or by calling pg_replication_origin_advance() with the next LSN after disabling the subscription or using disable_on_error; skipping the whole transaction can omit non-conflicting changes and make the subscriber inconsistent.

Source claim (L87): with streaming mode 'parallel', the finish LSN of failed transactions may not be logged; changing streaming to 'on' or 'off' and reproducing the conflicts may be needed to obtain it.

Inference: the page separates fatal conflicts (replication stops, manual action) from conflicts that are still applied or silently skipped, so pg_stat_subscription_stats counts are not equivalent to replication-stopping events.

sections: Extractor metadata: title, URL, published time and 'Markdown Content:' label (L1-7; excluded)
Physical-standby prerequisite, failover=true slot synchronization, and seamless subscription continuation after promotion (L8)
Asynchronous slot copying, the need to confirm synchronization before failover, and synchronized_standby_slots (L10)
Purpose of the three-step readiness verification (L12)
Step 1: subscriber query listing replication slots of failover-enabled subscriptions from pg_subscription (L14-24)
Step 2: per-database query for table synchronization slots whose copy finished, using pg_subscription_rel and pg_control_system (L25-38)
Step 3: standby check that slots exist and are failover-ready via synced, NOT temporary and invalidation_reason IS NULL (L39-51)
Interpretation: subscriptions may continue on the new primary when every slot is present and failover_ready is true (L53)
PostgreSQL versus non-PostgreSQL subscribers; run steps on each subscriber node served by the designated standby (L55)
Planned failover: primary-side query for all failover-enabled, non-temporary slots instead of steps 1-2 (L57-65)
notes: Source claim (L8): for subscribers to continue replicating after the publisher goes down, a physical standby corresponding to the publisher is required; logical slots for the subscriptions can be synchronized to the standby by specifying failover = true when creating subscriptions, referencing Section 47.2.3.

Source claim (L8): the failover parameter is said to ensure a seamless transition of those subscriptions after the standby is promoted, and they can continue subscribing to publications on the new primary.

Source claim (L10): slot synchronization copies asynchronously, so replication slots must be confirmed synced to the standby before failover; the standby must be ahead of the subscriber, which synchronized_standby_slots can achieve.

Source claim (L14-24): on the subscriber, pg_subscription rows with subfailover true and a non-null subslotname identify the replication slots that should be synced to the standby planned for promotion.

Source claim (L25-38): a second subscriber-side query, run on each database with failover-enabled subscriptions, derives table synchronization slot names from pg_subscription_rel rows with srsubstate = 'f' joined with pg_subscription and pg_control_system; such slots need syncing only when the table copy is finished, since otherwise they are dropped or recreated on the new primary.
Source claim (L39-51): on the standby, pg_replication_slots is queried for each slot name, and failover_ready is defined as synced AND NOT temporary AND invalidation_reason IS NULL.
Source claim (L53): if all slots are present on the standby and failover_ready is true, existing subscriptions can continue subscribing to publications on the new primary.

Source claim (L55): the first two steps are meant for a PostgreSQL subscriber and are recommended on each subscriber node that the designated standby will serve, so the complete slot list can be verified in step 3; non-PostgreSQL subscribers may use their own methods to identify their slots.

Source claim (L57-65): for planned failover, to confirm that all subscribers can continue after failover, a primary-side query over pg_replication_slots with failover true and NOT temporary returns the slots that need syncing, replacing steps 1-2.

Inference: the procedure verifies slot presence and synchronization state, not data freshness by itself; the 'standby ahead of subscriber' condition is delegated to synchronized_standby_slots rather than checked by the shown queries.
Inference: table synchronization slots are relevant only while a table copy is in progress; the page's state filter srsubstate = 'f' encodes that transient role.

Pre-18.0 behavior and the generated-column-to-regular-column use case (L33-35)

Opt-in mechanisms: publish_generated_columns = 'stored' or an explicit table column list (L41-47)

notes: Source claim (L8): typically the subscriber table is defined the same as the publisher, so a publisher GENERATED column has a matching subscriber generated column; in that case the subscriber table's generated-column value is always the one used.

Source claim (L10-31): the example publishes a table with b GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a + 1) STORED and inserts 1, 2, 3, producing b = 2, 3, 4 on the publisher; the subscriber defines b GENERATED ALWAYS AS (a * 100) STORED and shows b = 100, 200, 300, demonstrating that the subscriber recomputes locally.
Source claim (L33): prior to version 18.0, logical replication did not publish GENERATED columns at all.

Source claim (L35-39): replicating a generated column to a regular column can be desirable, and the Tip says this may be useful when replicating to a non-PostgreSQL database through an output plugin, especially if the target does not support generated columns.

Source claim (L41-47): generated columns are not published by default; users can opt in by setting the publication parameter publish_generated_columns to 'stored' (current and future stored generated columns) or by specifying a table column list that nominates stored generated columns.
Source claim (L49-51): when determining which columns are published, a column list takes precedence and overrides the publish_generated_columns parameter.

Source claim (L53-64): Table 29.2 gives six outcomes: unpublished GENERATED to GENERATED uses the subscriber's generated value; to regular uses the subscriber column default; to a missing column does nothing; published GENERATED to GENERATED is an unsupported ERROR; to regular replicates the publisher value; to a missing column is an ERROR reporting the column missing.

Source claim (L68-72): there is currently no support for subscriptions comprising several publications where the same table is published with different column lists; the same situation arises when one publication publishes generated columns and another in the same subscription does not.
Source claim (L74-76): if the subscriber is from a release prior to 18, initial table synchronization will not copy generated columns even when they are defined on the publisher.

Inference: enabling publication of generated columns is aimed at regular target columns; the generated-to-generated combination is explicitly unsupported rather than silently recomputed from replicated input.

Inference: because a column list overrides publish_generated_columns, mixing publications with and without that setting for one table can change the effective column set, which the warning treats as unsupported.

sections.heading: Publication-node monitoring by analogy to physical streaming replication

notes: Source claim (line 8): logical replication is based on a similar architecture to physical streaming replication, so monitoring on a publication node is similar to monitoring a physical replication primary; detail is deferred to Section 26.2.5.2.

Source claim (line 10): subscription monitoring information is visible in pg_stat_subscription, which contains one row for every subscription worker; a subscription can have zero or more active workers depending on its state.

Source claim (line 12): normally one apply process runs for an enabled subscription; a disabled or crashed subscription has zero rows; in-progress initial synchronization adds workers for the tables being synchronized; parallel apply of a streaming transaction can add parallel apply workers.

Inference (reader): the page defines worker presence as the observable and names no lag, byte, transaction, error or retention metric, so it cannot support claims about replication delay or retained WAL.
Inference (reader): zero rows conflates disabled and crashed subscriptions on this page, so worker count alone cannot separate intentional disablement from failure without state read elsewhere.

notes: Source claim (L8): the seven items are current restrictions or missing functionality, and the page says these might be addressed in future releases.

Source claim (L10): schema and DDL are not replicated; the initial schema can be copied with pg_dump --schema-only, later schema changes must be kept in sync manually, and schemas need not be identical. Replication errors while arriving data does not fit the subscriber schema; applying additive changes to the subscriber first often avoids intermittent errors.

Source claim (L12): sequence data is not replicated. Serial or identity column values replicate as table data, but the sequence on the subscriber still shows its start value. Read-only subscribers are usually unaffected; a switchover or failover requires updating sequences to the latest values by copying current data or choosing a sufficiently high value from the tables.

Source claim (L14): TRUNCATE is replicated, and the subscriber truncates the same explicitly specified or CASCADE-collected group minus tables outside the subscription. This works when all affected tables share one subscription, but fails when a table to be truncated has foreign-key links to tables outside the same or any subscription.

Source claim (L16, L18): large objects are not replicated and the only workaround is storing data in normal tables. Only tables, including partitioned tables, are supported; replicating views, materialized views or foreign tables results in an error.

Source claim (L20): partitioned replication originates by default from the publisher's leaf partitions, so those partitions must exist on the subscriber as valid target tables (leaf, further subpartitioned, or independent). publish_via_partition_root can instead replicate using the identity and schema of the partitioned root table.

Source claim (L22): with REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, UPDATE and DELETE cannot be applied on subscribers when tables include attributes whose types (such as point or box) lack a default operator class for B-tree or Hash; defining a primary key or replica identity overcomes this limitation.

Inference: the restrictions are stated as product behavior, not measured failure rates; the page reports no experiments, no version matrix beyond the current documentation, and no workaround beyond those named.
Inference: these constraints mark where table-row replication stops and where DDL, sequence state, large objects and non-table relations remain external operational responsibilities.

sections.heading: 29.2 Subscription: definition, topology and table matching (untitled introduction)
Example 1: connect = false, slot created manually
Example 2: connect = false with slot_name specified

notes: Source claim (L8-12): a subscription is the downstream side of logical replication; the node where it is defined is the subscriber; it defines a connection to another database plus one or more publications. The subscriber behaves like any PostgreSQL instance and can publish for others; a node may hold multiple subscriptions and a publisher-subscriber pair may have several, but care is required so subscribed publication objects do not overlap.

Source claim (L14-16): each subscription receives changes through one replication slot, with additional slots possibly needed for initial synchronization of pre-existing table data and dropped when synchronization ends. A subscription can act as a synchronous-replication standby; the standby name defaults to the subscription name and can be overridden by application_name in the connection string.

Source claim (L18-22): pg_dump dumps subscriptions only for a superuser, otherwise warns and skips them because non-superusers cannot read all subscription information from pg_subscription. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION adds a subscription, ALTER SUBSCRIPTION stops/resumes it, DROP SUBSCRIPTION removes it; dropping and recreating loses synchronization information, so data must be resynchronized.

Source claim (L24-28): schema definitions are not replicated and published tables must already exist on the subscriber; only regular tables can be replication targets, not views. Tables are matched by fully qualified name and columns by name (order may differ); types may differ if the text representation converts, e.g. integer to bigint; extra subscriber columns receive their declared defaults; binary-format replication is more restrictive.

Source claim (L32-36): each active subscription receives changes from a remote slot; table synchronization slots are normally transient, created internally for initial synchronization and dropped automatically, with generated names 'pg_%u_sync_%u_%llu' (subscription oid, table relid, system identifier). Normally the remote slot is created with CREATE SUBSCRIPTION and dropped with DROP SUBSCRIPTION.

Source claim (L38-44): slot management can be separated from subscription lifecycle. Use create_slot = false when the remote slot already exists; connect = false when the remote host is unreachable or unclear (pg_dump does this), requiring a manually created slot before activation; disassociate the slot with ALTER SUBSCRIPTION when moving the subscriber or when the remote is unreachable at drop time. An unreachable remote's slot (and leftover table sync slots) must be dropped manually, because it would keep reserving WAL and could fill the disk.

Source claim (L48-83): the setup example creates three tables with primary keys, publications pub1 (t1), pub2 (t2, publish = 'truncate'), pub3a (t3, publish = 'truncate') and pub3b (t3, row filter e > 5); subscription sub3 subscribes to both pub3a and pub3b, and all subscriptions copy initial data by default.

Source claim (L85-111, L154-182): initial table copying ignores the publication's publish operations and row filters - t2 is copied despite its truncate-only publication, and t3 receives all three initial rows despite pub3b's filter. During subsequent replication the publish operations and filter apply: the later inserts leave t2 at three rows and deliver only e = 6 to t3, giving t3 rows 1, 2, 3 and 6.

Source claim (L186-257): deferred slot creation requires creating the slot on the publisher with pg_create_logical_replication_slot(<slot_name>, 'pgoutput'), then ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... ENABLE and REFRESH PUBLICATION on the subscriber. SET (slot_name = 'myslot').

sections.heading: Range notation: worked examples and edge cases

notes: Source claim (lines 6-8): a shard is a subset of a keyspace; a keyspace always contains one or more shards; a shard typically contains one MySQL primary and potentially many MySQL replicas, which hold identical data apart from replication lag and can serve read-only traffic with eventual consistency, long-running analysis, and administrative tasks such as backup, restore and diff.

Source claim (line 10): an unsharded keyspace has exactly one shard, named '0' (sometimes '-') by convention; a sharded keyspace has N shards holding non-overlapping data, the shard count varies with use case and load, and some Vitess users run hundreds of shards in a keyspace.

Source claim (lines 12-19): shard names represent a range in unsigned integer space (left bound included, right bound excluded), are written in hexadecimal, are left-justified and right-padded with zeros; a '-' prefix means anything less than the right value, a '-' postfix means anything greater than or equal to the left value, and a plain '-' denotes the full keyrange.

Source claim (lines 21-27): '-80', '00-80', '0000-8000' and the sixteen-hex-digit form denote the same range; '80-FF' equals '8000-FF00', so 'FFFF' falls outside '80-FF'; consequently '80-' is not the same as '80-FF', and '80-' means anything greater than or equal to 0x80.

Source claim (line 29): an xxhash-type vindex produces an unsigned 64-bit integer, so every value below 0x8000000000000000 falls in shard '-80' and every value with the highest bit set belongs to shard '80-'.

Source claim (lines 31-35): the left-justified encoding permits keyspace IDs of arbitrary length with the most significant bits on the left; an md5 hash (16 bytes) can serve as a keyspace ID, and an arbitrary-length varbinary can be mapped as-is by the 'binary' vindex.

Source claim (lines 37-39): resharding changes the shard count on a live cluster by splitting shards into smaller pieces or merging neighbouring shards; source data is copied to destination shards, allowed to catch up on replication, compared against the original for integrity, live serving is shifted, and the source shards are deleted.

Inference (reader, not stated on the page): the page defines a shard simultaneously as a keyrange and as a MySQL replication group, but says nothing about where topology and routing metadata live, how the cutover in resharding is coordinated, or what read consistency holds across shards, so mechanism-level claims about those need other sources.

Scope and artifacts: no section headings exist on the page, so sections above are reader-supplied labels; the footer link block and the trailing '* * *' separator (lines 41-45) were excluded; the doubled hyphen in '80-FF' and the quote characters are preserved as captured.

sections.heading: Overview: startup, SQL/KV conversion, ranges and replication
CockroachDB architecture terms: Raft protocol, Raft leader, Raft log

notes: Source claim (L42): CockroachDB was designed as a database that is both scalable and consistent; the guide explains its inner workings as a high-level framework for serious users and database enthusiasts, and understanding the architecture is not required to use the product.

Source claim (L45): the guide is organized by architecture layers and is meant to be read sequentially, starting with this overview and then the next layer page (label elided); the Overview section of each layer is enough for a high-level understanding while Components sections add technical detail for readers such as contributors; the guide does not explain how to build applications on CockroachDB.

Source claim (L47-L58): stated goals are low-touch, highly automated operation and simple reasoning for two audiences (audience labels elided); industry-leading consistency at scale, including distributed transactions and avoiding eventual-consistency and stale-read problems; always-on reads and writes on all nodes without conflicts; flexible deployment without platform or vendor lock-in; and familiar relational tooling (the parenthetical example is elided).

Source claim (L60-L69): a cluster starts from a command carrying --join for every initial node plus a one-time initialization command (both command names elided). Clients use a SQL API; any node accepts statements, converts SQL RPCs into KV operations and splits data into ranges; each range is replicated for survivability (count elided at L65; L118 states three copies by default); a node forwards requests it cannot serve; range changes commit through a consensus protocol (name elided); an efficient storage engine (name elided) tracks timestamps and enables a SQL standard historical-read clause (name elided).

Source claim (L71-L72): architecture is presented as five layers, each relatively opaque to its neighbours: (1) translate SQL queries to KV operations, (2) allow atomic changes to multiple KV entries, (3) present replicated KV ranges as a single entity, (4) consistently and synchronously replicate ranges and enable consistent reads through consensus, (5) read and write KV data on disk. The table is flattened and the layer-name column is not retained.

Source claim (L77-L81): consistency requires a transaction to change affected data only in allowed ways, used in both ACID and CAP senses but less formally than either; isolation is the degree to which a transaction may be affected by concurrent transactions; CockroachDB provides SERIALIZABLE and READ COMMITTED (the cross-reference label is elided).

Source claim (L83-L87): consensus is agreement on whether a transaction is committed or aborted, implemented with Raft; a write is acknowledged by a quorum of nodes holding replicas, so a majority agrees on state even if some nodes are offline; without consensus forward progress halts to preserve consistency; replication requires writes to propagate to a quorum of copies before commit.

Source claim (L89-L97): a transaction is a set of operations satisfying ACID; contention appears as lock contention (a transaction unable to complete because another concurrent or recent transaction writes the same data) or as a serialization conflict (a transaction that could not be placed into an ordering among currently executing transactions); automatic retry may follow, and if retry is impossible or fails an error is emitted that requires a client under SERIALIZABLE isolation to retry (several nouns and the remediation steps at L97 are elided).

Source claim (L99-L103): multi-active availability is a consensus-based notion in which each node handles reads and writes for a per-range subset, contrasted with active-passive (one active node receives all traffic) and active-active (all nodes accept requests but reads are typically not both current and fast); a SQL user is an identity that authenticates by password, SSO or certificate and is distinct from a Cloud organization user.

Source claim (L108-L130): a cluster is interconnected nodes acting as one distributed SQL server with its own authorization hierarchy; a node is one instance; a range is a contiguous chunk of the sorted KV keyspace, with a table and its secondary indexes initially mapping to one range that splits when it reaches an elided size; a replica is a copy on a node (three by default); the leaseholder coordinates all reads and writes for a range, is for most tables the only replica serving consistent reads, and equals the Raft leader except briefly during an elided event; the Raft leader uses the log to confirm a majority; the Raft log is the on-disk source of truth for replication.

sections: 6 Runtime View (Content: scenario areas and the architectural-relevance selection criterion)
Motivation (understand how building-block instances perform work and communicate at runtime; scenarios for stakeholders less able to read static models)
Form (notations: numbered natural-language steps, activity diagrams or flow charts, sequence diagrams, BPMN or EPCs, state machines, ...)

notes: Source claim: the runtime view describes concrete behavior and interactions of the system's building blocks in the form of scenarios from important use cases or features (how building blocks execute them), interactions at critical external interfaces (how building blocks cooperate with users and neighbouring systems), operation and administration (launch, start-up, stop), and error and exception scenarios.

Source claim: the main criterion for choosing scenarios is their architectural relevancy; describing a large number of scenarios is not important, and a representative selection should be documented instead.

Source claim: the reader should understand how instances of building blocks perform their job and communicate at runtime, mainly to communicate the architecture to stakeholders who are less willing or able to read the static models (building block view, deployment view).

Source claim: many notations are possible - a numbered list of steps in natural language, activity diagrams or flow charts, sequence diagrams, BPMN or EPCs, state machines - and the list ends with an ellipsis, so it is not exhaustive.

Source claim: the 6.1 scenario template asks for a runtime diagram or textual description of the scenario plus a description of the notable aspects of the interactions between the building-block instances depicted; sections 6.2 to 6.n repeat the same pattern.

Source claim: eleven practical tips are listed as link titles: map existing building blocks to activities (6-1), document only a few scenarios (6-2), document schematic rather than detailed scenarios (6-3), document detailed scenarios with caution (6-4), use scenarios primarily to discover building blocks rather than for documentation (6-5), describe excerpts or partial scenarios (6-6), use activity diagrams with swimlanes (6-7) or partitions (6-8), use a textual notation (6-9), use both small and large building blocks (6-10), and use sequence diagrams (6-11).

Source claim: the page links related FAQ questions, the runtime views of real systems, and three worked examples (HTML Sanity Checker, MaMa, TrafficPursuitUnit); those linked pages are outside this unit and were not read.

Inference: tips 6-2 and 6-3 (few, schematic scenarios) pull against 6-4 and 6-11 (detailed scenarios, sequence diagrams); the page gives no tie-breaker beyond architectural relevance and the warning to use detail with caution.

Inference: unlike the tables in sections 4 and 5, the runtime template defines no fields for preconditions, triggers, outcomes or failure handling; the only required elements are a diagram or textual description and a note on notable interaction aspects.
